title: Emergency Action Plan
applicability: Required whenever another OSHA standard in Part 1910 requires one (e.g., PSM, HAZWOPER, several substance standards). Best practice for any facility. May be oral if 10 or fewer employees.
required_elements: Procedures for reporting a fire or other emergency
Emergency evacuation procedures and route assignments (floor plans/maps)
Procedures for employees who remain to operate critical operations before they evacuate
Procedures to account for all employees after evacuation
Rescue and medical duties for those performing them
Name/job title of persons to contact for further information
An employee alarm system compliant with 1910.165
training: Train enough employees to assist in safe/orderly evacuation; review the plan with each employee at assignment and when duties/plan change.
recordkeeping: Keep the written plan in the workplace, available to employees.
failure_points: No evacuation map or assembly point named
No headcount/accountability procedure
No named contacts
Alarm system not described or not 1910.165-compliant
notes: Low-difficulty program — should always score A. Often paired with the Fire Prevention Plan.

title: Fire Prevention Plan
applicability: Required when another OSHA standard requires one (e.g., ethylene oxide, MDA, 1,3-butadiene). Best practice broadly. May be oral if 10 or fewer employees.
required_elements: List of all major fire hazards, proper handling/storage of hazardous materials, potential ignition sources and their control
Type of fire protection equipment to control each major hazard
Procedures to control accumulation of flammable/combustible waste
Procedures for regular maintenance of heat-producing equipment safeguards
Name/job title of employees responsible for maintaining fire-control equipment and for control of fuel-source hazards
training: Inform employees of the fire hazards of the materials/processes they are exposed to; review the plan at assignment.
recordkeeping: Keep written plan in the workplace, available to employees.
failure_points: Fire hazards not itemized for the specific facility
No named person responsible for equipment maintenance
Housekeeping/waste-control procedures missing

title: Occupational Noise Exposure / Hearing Conservation Program
applicability: A written/administered Hearing Conservation Program (HCP) is required when employee noise exposure equals or exceeds an 8-hour TWA of 85 dBA (the action level).
required_elements: Noise exposure monitoring and employee notification of results
Audiometric testing program (baseline within 6 months, annual audiograms, standard threshold shift follow-up)
Hearing protector selection, provision, and required use; attenuation adequacy
Employee training program (annual): effects of noise, purpose of protectors, purpose of audiometric testing
Access to information and recordkeeping
training: Annual training for all employees exposed at or above the 85 dBA action level.
recordkeeping: Retain noise exposure measurement records 2 years; audiometric test records for duration of the affected employee's employment.
failure_points: No baseline/annual audiograms documented
No monitoring data establishing who is in the program
Training not conducted annually
Standard threshold shift procedures missing

title: Process Safety Management of Highly Hazardous Chemicals (PSM)
applicability: Applies to processes involving a threshold quantity of a listed highly hazardous chemical, or 10,000 lb of a flammable liquid/gas. Core for refineries, gas plants, chemical facilities.
required_elements: Employee Participation — written plan of action for involving employees (1910.119(c))
Process Safety Information — chemical, technology, and equipment data (d)
Process Hazard Analysis — using a recognized methodology; revalidate at least every 5 years (e)
Operating Procedures — written, for each covered process, incl. startup/normal/emergency (f)
Training — initial and refresher on procedures and hazards (g)
Contractors — selection, training, and oversight of contract employees (h)
Pre-Startup Safety Review before new/modified processes (i)
Mechanical Integrity — inspection, testing, maintenance of critical equipment (j)
Hot Work Permit system (k)
Management of Change — written procedure for process/equipment/procedure changes (l)
Incident Investigation — within 48 hours; document findings and corrective actions (m)
Emergency Planning and Response (n)
Compliance Audits — at least every 3 years (o)
Trade Secrets provisions (p)
training: Initial training on the process and refresher at least every 3 years (documented). Contractors trained on process hazards and the facility EAP.
recordkeeping: Retain PHAs and updates for the life of the process; incident reports 5 years.
failure_points: PHA not revalidated within 5 years
Operating procedures not covering emergency shutdown
MOC used as replacement-in-kind loophole
Contractor element (h) ignored — this is where prequalified contractors are graded
Compliance audit older than 3 years
notes: Contractors are usually asked for the elements that touch them (h), plus their own hot-work, MOC awareness, and incident-investigation programs.

title: Hazardous Waste Operations and Emergency Response (HAZWOPER)
applicability: Applies to cleanup operations at hazardous waste sites, RCRA TSD facilities, and emergency response to hazardous-substance releases. Construction analog is 1926.65.
required_elements: Written safety and health program per 1910.120(b): organizational structure, comprehensive workplan, site-specific safety and health plan (HASP), safety and health training program, medical surveillance program, SOPs, and coordination with contractors

Site-specific HASP per (b)(4)(ii): hazard analysis for each task, employee training assignments, PPE selection, medical surveillance, air monitoring, site control, decon procedures, emergency response plan, confined-space entry, spill containment
Site control program: site map, work zones, buddy system, communications, nearest medical assistance
Emergency Response Plan (ERP) per (l) or (q) for responders
Written PPE program
training: 40-hr (general site workers) / 24-hr (occasional) initial + 8-hr annual refresher; 8-hr supervisor training. Responders trained to the appropriate level (awareness through specialist).
recordkeeping: Medical surveillance and training records retained per 1910.1020 (duration of employment + 30 years).
failure_points: HASP not site-specific (generic boilerplate)
No documented 40-hour/24-hour training + 8-hour refresher
Medical surveillance not tied to exposure
ERP missing for emergency responders (q)

title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) — Hazard Assessment
applicability: Applies to all general-industry workplaces. A written certification of the hazard assessment is mandatory even though the PPE 'program' itself need not be a single document.
required_elements: Written certification of a workplace hazard assessment: identifies the workplace evaluated, the person certifying, the date, and identifies the document as a certification of hazard assessment (1910.132(d)(2))
PPE selection based on the assessment for each hazard
Requirement that PPE be provided at no cost (with narrow exceptions)
Employee training on PPE use per 1910.132(f)
Cleaning, maintenance, and replacement provisions
training: Train each employee who must use PPE: when/what PPE is necessary, how to don/doff/adjust/wear, limitations, and care. Retrain on changes.
recordkeeping: Keep the written hazard-assessment certification; verification of training (name + date).
failure_points: Missing the signed/dated written hazard-assessment certification — the #1 PPE citation
No documented training with the required content
Eye/face, head, foot, hand hazards not individually assessed

title: Respiratory Protection Program
applicability: Required whenever respirators are necessary to protect employee health, or the employer requires respirator use. A written program with worksite-specific procedures is mandatory.
required_elements: Written program administered by a suitably trained program administrator
Procedures for selecting respirators based on workplace hazards
Medical evaluation of employees before fit testing/use (mandatory questionnaire or exam)
Fit testing procedures (initial and annual) for tight-fitting respirators
Procedures for proper use in routine and emergency/IDLH situations
Cartridge change schedule / end-of-service-life indicators
Cleaning, disinfecting, storage, inspection, repair, maintenance
Air quality standards for supplied-air respirators
Training on respiratory hazards, proper use, and limitations
Program evaluation procedures
training: Annual training and annual fit testing; medical evaluation before use and when conditions change.
recordkeeping: Retain medical evaluation records (per 1910.1020) and current fit-test records; retain the written program.
failure_points: No named program administrator
Medical evaluation skipped or not before fit test
Annual fit test not documented
No change-out schedule for chemical cartridges
Voluntary-use employees not given Appendix D

title: Permit-Required Confined Spaces (General Industry)
applicability: Applies where the workplace contains permit-required confined spaces. Construction uses 1926 Subpart AA (1926.1200).
required_elements: Written permit-space program
Means to identify and evaluate permit spaces; signage/informing employees
Permit system (entry permit content, duration, cancellation)
Atmospheric testing order: oxygen, then flammable, then toxic; continuous monitoring where needed
Roles: authorized entrants, attendants, entry supervisors and their duties
Ventilation, isolation, and hazard control procedures
Rescue and emergency services — non-entry retrieval preferred; verify rescue capability
Coordination with contractors/host employer
training: Train entrants, attendants, and supervisors on duties, hazards, and rescue; retrain on changes or deficiencies.
recordkeeping: Retain cancelled entry permits at least 1 year for program review.
failure_points: Testing order not specified (O2/flammable/toxic)
Rescue plan relies on 911 without verifying response capability
No attendant duties defined
Reclassification/alternate-entry procedures misused

title: Control of Hazardous Energy (Lockout/Tagout)
applicability: Applies to servicing/maintenance of machines where unexpected energization or release of stored energy could cause injury.
required_elements: Written energy control program with energy-control procedures, employee training, and periodic inspection
Machine/equipment-specific energy control procedures (steps for shutting down, isolating, blocking, securing; placement/removal of devices; testing to verify de-energization)
Annual periodic inspection of each energy-control procedure, documented, by an authorized employee not using the procedure
Roles of authorized vs. affected employees
Provisions for group lockout, shift change, and contractor coordination
Requirements for locks/tags/devices (durable, standardized, substantial, identifiable)
training: Authorized, affected, and other employees trained to their role; retrain on job/procedure changes or inspection deficiencies.
recordkeeping: Document the annual periodic inspection (procedure, date, employees, inspector).
failure_points: Missing the documented ANNUAL periodic inspection — the classic F
Only a generic policy with no machine-specific procedures
No procedure for verifying de-energization (try-out step)
Group and contractor LOTO not addressed

title: Powered Industrial Trucks (Forklift Program)
applicability: Applies wherever powered industrial trucks (forklifts, order pickers, etc.) are used.
required_elements: Operator training and evaluation program (formal instruction, practical training, and workplace evaluation)
Operator re-evaluation at least every 3 years
Refresher training after an accident/near-miss, unsafe operation, condition change, or new equipment type
Daily/pre-shift inspection procedure and removal-from-service of unsafe trucks
Truck-type and workplace-specific operating hazards addressed
training: Combination of formal + practical training and an evaluation; re-evaluate every 3 years and after triggering events.
recordkeeping: Certify operator training/evaluation (name, dates, evaluator).
failure_points: Missing the 3-year operator re-evaluation
No documented practical evaluation (classroom only)
Daily inspection not documented

title: Electrical Safety-Related Work Practices
related_citations: NFPA 70E (2024) — consensus arc-flash / electrical safe work method
29 CFR 1910.303-.308 (Subpart S design/installation, incl. arc-flash label duty at .303)
applicability: Applies to qualified and unqualified persons who work on, near, or with exposed energized parts operating at 50 volts or more. OSHA 1910.331-.335 sets the mandatory safe-work-practice duty; NFPA 70E is the consensus method OSHA and every prequal reviewer expect an employer to follow to satisfy it (boundaries, incident-energy analysis, arc-rated PPE, EEWP). Below 50 V, de-energized work is the default and 70E's boundary/PPE machinery generally does not attach.
required_elements: De-energize first: establishing an electrically safe work condition (ESWC) is the default; energized work is allowed only where de-energizing introduces a greater hazard or is infeasible, and that justification is documented

Energized Electrical Work Permit (EEWP) process for any permitted energized work inside the arc-flash or restricted approach boundary, with the exemptions (e.g., testing/troubleshooting/diagnostics by a qualified person in properly rated PPE) defined
Lockout/tagout coordination with 1910.147 for electrical isolation, plus the ESWC verification steps (test-before-touch with an adequately rated meter proven on a known source)
Shock risk assessment: identify voltage, determine the limited and restricted approach boundaries, and select shock PPE (rated gloves, insulated tools)
Arc-flash risk assessment: determine the arc-flash boundary and either incident energy (cal/cm2) by engineering analysis or the 70E PPE-category (table) method — one method per task, never mixed
Arc-rated (AR) PPE and insulated tools selected to the assessed hazard; face/head/hand/body protection; no meltable synthetics underneath
Equipment arc-flash labeling per 1910.303(e)/(f) and 70E 130.5(H): nominal voltage, arc-flash boundary, and incident energy (or PPE category)
Qualified vs. unqualified person definitions, with only qualified persons permitted to cross the restricted approach boundary or perform energized work
Job briefing before energized work covering hazards, procedures, boundaries, PPE, and emergency response
training: Qualified persons: trained and demonstrably able to identify and avoid energized parts, determine nominal voltage, use the required PPE and insulated tools, and apply approach boundaries; retrain at least every three years and after any change in equipment, procedure, or after an audit finds a deficiency. Unqualified persons: trained in the related practices necessary for their safety (staying outside boundaries). Document topic, date, trainer, and employee with a signature or LMS record.
recordkeeping: Keep: the written electrical safety program and its annual audit; the incident-energy / arc-flash study and equipment label list; EEWPs (retain per company policy, commonly the equipment life or a set term); qualified-person training records with retrain dates; and PPE inspection/rubber-goods test records (insulating gloves tested on a 6-month cycle).
failure_points: No arc-flash study / no incident-energy or PPE-category basis for boundaries
Equipment not labeled with arc-flash boundary and incident energy (or PPE category)
Energized work performed with no EEWP or no documented infeasibility justification
Mixing the incident-energy method and the PPE-category table method on the same task
Qualified-person training not documented or older than the 3-year retrain cycle
No annual program audit / no field observation of work practices (70E 110.5(M))
source: https://www.osha.gov/electrical  (NFPA 70E is the consensus arc-flash method OSHA references; buy the standard at nfpa.org/70E)
notes: This is the anchor written program for electrical safety. NFPA 70E is copyrighted — Origin states requirements, thresholds, and procedures in its own words and cites the section, and points the user to the actual 70E table (e.g., 130.5(G) PPE-category and 130.7(C)(15) PPE tables) rather than reproducing them. Related granular topics are broken out as their own KB records (ESWC, boundaries, arc-flash assessment, AR PPE, EEWP, labeling, qualified-person training, and the ESP audit duty).

title: Welding, Cutting, and Brazing / Hot Work
applicability: Applies to welding, cutting, brazing, grinding, and other spark/flame-producing work. Overlaps PSM hot-work (1910.119(k)) at covered processes.
required_elements: Hot-work permit system (authorization, scope, duration)
Fire prevention/protection precautions and combustible clearance (35 ft) or shielding
Fire watch during work and for at least 30 minutes after
Confined-space and atmospheric considerations
Ventilation and respiratory protection for fumes/gases
Cylinder handling and storage requirements
training: Train personnel on safe operation, fire prevention, permit use, and fire-watch duties.
failure_points: No fire-watch requirement (during + 30 min after)
Permit system not described
Combustible clearance distance omitted

title: Bloodborne Pathogens — Exposure Control Plan
applicability: Applies where employees have reasonably anticipated occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials (incl. designated first-aid responders).
required_elements: Written Exposure Control Plan, reviewed and updated at least annually
Exposure determination (job classifications/tasks with occupational exposure) without regard to PPE
Methods of compliance: universal precautions, engineering and work-practice controls, PPE
Hepatitis B vaccination offered free within 10 days of assignment
Post-exposure evaluation and follow-up procedures
Communication of hazards (labels/signs) and training
Sharps injury log and consideration of safer devices
training: Initial and annual training for employees with occupational exposure.
recordkeeping: Medical records for duration of employment + 30 years; training records 3 years; sharps injury log.
failure_points: Plan not reviewed/updated annually (missing current date)
Exposure determination missing or done 'with PPE' assumption
No documented HBV vaccination offer/declination

title: Hazard Communication (HazCom / GHS)
applicability: Applies to every workplace where employees may be exposed to hazardous chemicals. The most commonly required program of all. Construction cross-references it at 1926.59.
required_elements: Written hazard communication program
A list/inventory of the hazardous chemicals known to be present (by identity used on the SDS)
Methods for maintaining and providing access to Safety Data Sheets (SDS)
Container labeling system for workplace containers
Employee information and training program
Methods to inform employees of non-routine task hazards and hazards of chemicals in unlabeled pipes
For multi-employer worksites, how SDSs and precautions are shared with other employers
training: Train at initial assignment and whenever a new hazard is introduced: hazards, protective measures, SDS/label reading, and the written program's location.
recordkeeping: Maintain the written program, chemical inventory, and SDSs accessible to employees each shift.
failure_points: Generic plan that never lists the company's own chemicals
No named program administrator/responsible person
SDS access method not described
Secondary/workplace container labeling omitted
notes: If you fix only one program, fix this. It is requested in essentially every contractor requirement set.

title: Laboratory Chemical Hygiene Plan
applicability: Applies to laboratories that use hazardous chemicals on a laboratory scale (the 'lab standard').
required_elements: Written Chemical Hygiene Plan (CHP), reviewed/evaluated at least annually
Designation of a Chemical Hygiene Officer
SOPs for work with hazardous chemicals
Criteria for control measures (fume hoods, PPE) and their maintenance
Provisions for medical consultation/exams
Employee information and training
Provisions for particularly hazardous substances (select carcinogens, reproductive toxins, acute toxins)
training: Train lab workers on the CHP, chemical hazards, detection, and protective measures.
failure_points: No Chemical Hygiene Officer named
CHP not reviewed annually
Fume-hood performance not addressed

title: Asbestos (General Industry)
applicability: Applies where employee exposure to airborne asbestos fibers occurs at or above the action level / as defined by the standard.
required_elements: Written compliance program to reduce exposure to or below the PEL using engineering and work-practice controls (with an implementation schedule)
Exposure monitoring / assessment and employee notification of results
Establishment of regulated areas where the PEL is exceeded (where required)

Hygiene facilities and housekeeping practices

recordkeeping: Exposure and medical records retained per 1910.1020 (generally duration of employment + 30 years).
failure_points: No written compliance program with an engineering-control schedule

title: Access to Employee Exposure and Medical Records
applicability: Applies wherever employee exposure or medical records are created; governs retention and employee access to those records.
required_elements: Procedures granting employees/representatives access to their exposure and medical records within 15 working days
Retention: employee medical records for duration of employment + 30 years; exposure records 30 years
Preservation and transfer of records; informing employees of their rights annually
Designation of records custodian
failure_points: Records not retained for the full 30-year period
Employees not informed of access rights

title: Recording and Reporting Occupational Injuries and Illnesses
applicability: Applies to most employers with more than 10 employees at any point in the prior calendar year, unless the establishment is in a partially exempt low-hazard industry (1904.2, Appendix A to Subpart B). All employers, regardless of size or exemption, must still report severe injuries under 1904.39. These logs are the raw data prequal platforms convert into the TRIR, DART, and (with the mod worksheet) the EMR they grade a contractor on.
required_elements: Determine work-relatedness (1904.5) and whether the case is a new case (1904.6) before deciding recordability

Apply the general recording criteria (1904.7): record if the case involves death, days away from work, restricted work or job transfer, medical treatment beyond first aid, loss of consciousness, or a significant injury/illness diagnosed by a licensed health care professional
OSHA 300 Log — enter each recordable case within 7 calendar days of learning of it; classify the most serious outcome; count calendar days away / restricted (cap 180)
OSHA 301 Incident Report (or equivalent, e.g., a workers' comp first report) completed within 7 calendar days
Privacy concern cases (1904.29(b)(6-9)): omit the employee name from the 300 Log and keep a separate confidential list
OSHA 300A Annual Summary — review the log, total the columns, certify by a company executive, and post from February 1 to April 30 even if there were zero recordables
Severe-injury reporting (1904.39): fatality within 8 hours; in-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye within 24 hours

Electronic submission via the ITA (1904.41) for covered establishments — 300A for 20-249 employees in designated industries, and 300/301/300A for establishments with 100+ employees in the highest-hazard industries, by March 2 each year
Retain the 300, 300A, and 301 for 5 years following the year they cover and update the 300/300A during that period as new information arises (1904.33)
training: The recordkeeper (and any backup) should be trained on the 1904.5/.7 decision tree, the first-aid list, day counting, privacy cases, and the reporting timeframes, since inconsistent recordability decisions are the single biggest driver of a wrong TRIR.
recordkeeping: Retain OSHA 300, 300A, and 301 forms for 5 years following the calendar year each covers; keep the current-year 300 Log current within 7 days of learning of a case; retain the separate privacy-case list confidentially; keep ITA submission confirmations.
failure_points: 300A not certified by a company executive
Late severe-injury reporting
Recordability decisions inconsistent (drives inflated/deflated TRIR)
notes: Prequal platforms compute TRIR/DART/LTIR from these logs and EMR from the carrier's mod worksheet — accuracy here directly moves a contractor's score. This is the reference anchor; the recordability decision, the 300A, severe-injury reporting, ITA e-filing, and retention are broken out as their own KB records, and a fillable OSHA Recordkeeping Program is available as a written program.

title: General Safety and Health Provisions / Accident Prevention
applicability: Applies to all construction work. Establishes the employer's duty to have an accident-prevention program and competent-person inspections.
required_elements: Accident-prevention program providing for frequent and regular jobsite inspections by competent persons
Designation of competent persons for each applicable hazard
Instruction of each employee to recognize and avoid unsafe conditions and the regulations applicable to their work
Prompt removal/guarding of hazards
Only trained/authorized operators of equipment
failure_points: No competent person designated
No documented regular jobsite inspections
Employee hazard-recognition instruction not evidenced
notes: Reviewers treat this as the umbrella construction safety program; it signals overall program maturity.

title: Fall Protection (Construction)
applicability: Applies to construction work with fall exposures. General trigger height is 6 feet to a lower level (with activity-specific exceptions).
required_elements: Fall hazard assessment for each work area/task
Selection of fall protection systems (guardrails, safety nets, personal fall arrest, positioning, warning lines, controlled access zones)
Written Fall Protection Plan where conventional systems are infeasible (leading edge, precast, residential) — 1926.502(k)
Rescue plan for a worker suspended in a harness (prompt rescue)
Competent-person designation and equipment inspection
Training program per 1926.503 with written certification
training: Train each exposed employee to recognize fall hazards and use systems; written certification (name, date, trainer). Retrain on changes.
failure_points: No prompt-rescue plan for suspended workers — most-missed element
6-ft trigger not stated (or wrong trigger for the activity)
Training certification record missing
Written plan absent where conventional protection is infeasible

title: Scaffolding
applicability: Applies to all scaffolds used in construction. Fall-protection trigger for scaffolds is 10 feet.
required_elements: Scaffold erection/dismantling under supervision of a competent person by trained/experienced workers
Design by a qualified person; capacity at least 4x intended load
Fall protection at 10 feet (guardrails and/or PFAS)
Access provisions (ladders, stair towers) — cross-braces are not acceptable access
Competent-person inspection before each work shift and after any event affecting integrity
Training for erectors and users
training: Train users to recognize scaffold hazards; train erectors/dismantlers to a higher standard. Retrain on changes.
failure_points: 10-ft scaffold trigger confused with 6-ft general trigger
No pre-shift competent-person inspection
Access requirements not specified

title: Excavation and Trenching
applicability: Applies to all excavations and trenches in construction. Protective systems required at 5 feet or deeper (or shallower if a competent person identifies a hazard).
required_elements: Protective system (sloping/benching, shoring, or shielding/trench box) selected per soil classification
Soil classification by a competent person
Daily competent-person inspections before entry and as conditions change (rain, vibration)
Underground utility location before digging
Safe means of egress within 25 ft of workers in trenches 4 ft+
Atmospheric testing where hazardous atmospheres may exist (>4 ft)
Protection from spoil piles, water accumulation, and adjacent structures
training: Train the competent person on soil classification, protective systems, and hazard recognition.
failure_points: Competent-person daily inspection not documented — the enforcement hot spot
No soil classification
Utility locate step omitted
Egress ladder distance not addressed

title: Steel Erection
applicability: Applies to structural steel erection. Requires a site-specific erection plan and connector fall protection.
required_elements: Site-specific erection plan (SSEP) where required
Pre-planning: controlling contractor provides written notification of concrete strength and site-layout for cranes/equipment
Fall protection for connectors and in controlled decking zones (CDZ)
Column anchorage (4 anchor rods) and stability requirements
Fall protection at 15 feet for ironworkers (activity-specific)
training: Train erectors on fall hazards, CDZ procedures, and the SSEP.
failure_points: No site-specific erection plan
Connector/CDZ fall protection not addressed

title: EMR — Experience Modification Rate
applicability: A workers' compensation premium multiplier assigned to any employer whose payroll/premium exceeds the state eligibility threshold. Compares an employer's ACTUAL losses to EXPECTED losses for its class codes over a 3-year experience period (lagged ~1 year, most recent policy year excluded). 1.00 = industry-average; below 1.00 = credit (safer than peers), above 1.00 = debit. Rated by NCCI in ~35+ states; independent bureaus rate the rest (e.g., California/WCIRB, New York/NYCIRB, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, Wisconsin, and monopolistic states OH/ND/WA/WY).
required_elements: Payroll by class code for the 3-year experience period
Expected Loss Rate (ELR) per $100 payroll, published by the rating bureau per class code
D-Ratio (discount ratio) per class code — splits expected losses into primary vs. excess
Split point — the per-claim dollar cap dividing each claim into primary (capped, full weight) and excess (dampened) loss
Actual incurred losses, split into primary and excess (medical-only claims reduced to 30% of primary)
Weighting value (W) and Ballast value (B) from the bureau credibility tables, based on total expected losses
failure_points: Payroll misclassified to a higher-hazard class code, inflating expected losses
Open/reserved claims carried at inflated reserves not reviewed before unit-stat filing
Failing to dispute unit statistical data errors within the correction window
Claim frequency (many small claims) — hurts more than one large claim because primary losses carry full weight
Submitting an EMR without the matching rating-bureau worksheet when a hiring client asks for verification
notes: EMR is calculated by the rating bureau/carrier, not self-reported — but contractors must UNDERSTAND it to (a) reduce it and (b) explain an elevated mod to a hiring client. Reduction levers: aggressive return-to-work/light-duty (converts lost-time claims to medical-only), claims management and reserve review, safety program that cuts FREQUENCY, and auditing payroll class codes. The single most impactful because frequency drives primary losses.
formula:
Mod = ( Ap + W·Ae + B ) / ( Ep + W·Ee + B )
  Ap = actual primary losses (capped at split point)
  Ae = actual excess losses (above split point)
  Ep = expected primary losses (= expected losses × D-ratio)
  Ee = expected excess losses (= expected losses − expected primary)
  W  = weighting value (rises with employer size)
  B  = ballast value (stabilizes toward 1.00)
Expected losses by class = (Payroll ÷ 100) × ELR, summed across all class codes.
NCCI's simplified/split-plan form (post-2017): Mod ≈ ( Ap + Ee ) ÷ E, where the primary/excess weighting is pre-built into the bureau's limited rating factors.
calc_example: Employer with $200,000 expected losses; $88,100 actual primary and $75,640 actual excess (total actual $163,740); W = 0.16, B = $45,900. Plug primary at full weight and excess at the weighted rate into the formula → a mod near or below 1.00 yields a premium credit. A $100,000 manual premium × EMR 0.85 = $85,000 (saves $15,000/yr); × EMR 1.30 = $130,000.
benchmarks: 1.00 = industry average. Many oil & gas / construction operators require EMR < 1.00 to bid; some petrochemical owners cut off at 1.0 hard, others allow up to ~1.25 with a corrective plan. Below 0.80 is considered excellent. EMR is one of the three stats (with TRIR and DART) that prequalification platforms score.

title: TRIR — Total Recordable Incident Rate
applicability: The headline OSHA rate: all recordable injuries and illnesses per 100 full-time-equivalent workers per year. Used by every prequalification platform and most GCs as a first-pass safety screen. Computed from the OSHA 300 log and total hours worked.
required_elements: Count of OSHA-recordable cases (any case meeting 1904.7: death, days away, restricted/transfer, medical treatment beyond first aid, loss of consciousness, or significant diagnosis)
Total hours actually worked by all employees in the period (do NOT use 2,000×headcount if actual hours are available; exclude vacation/leave)
200,000-hour base constant (100 employees × 40 hrs × 50 weeks)
failure_points: Using scheduled hours instead of hours actually worked
Counting first-aid-only cases as recordable (over-counting) OR omitting recordable restricted-duty cases (under-counting)
Rate that doesn't reconcile to the submitted OSHA 300A totals
Three-year trend inconsistent with the 300A logs on file
notes: TRIR is self-reported but must tie exactly to the OSHA 300A logs the contractor uploads. Platforms score the 3-year TRIR against the NAICS benchmark; a rate above the industry average with no improvement trend is a common grade downgrade.
formula: TRIR = ( Number of OSHA-recordable cases × 200,000 ) ÷ Total hours worked
calc_example: 8 recordable cases over 430,000 hours worked → (8 × 200,000) ÷ 430,000 = 3.72 TRIR.
benchmarks: BLS Survey of Occupational Injuries & Illnesses (SOII), 2024 data (released Jan 2026): all private industry ≈ 2.3–2.7; Construction (NAICS 23) ≈ 2.3–2.5; Oil & gas extraction (NAICS 211) ≈ 0.8–1.4; Support activities for O&G (213112) ≈ 1.6; Manufacturing ≈ 2.8–3.2; Transportation & warehousing ≈ 4.0–4.8. Rates update annually — always pull the CURRENT BLS figure for the contractor's specific NAICS. Many GCs set a hard bid cutoff of TRIR < 1.0–2.0.

title: DART — Days Away, Restricted, or Transferred Rate
applicability: A severity-weighted rate: only the more serious cases — those resulting in days away from work, restricted duty, or job transfer — per 100 FTE. Always ≤ TRIR (it is a subset). Distinguishes serious injuries from minor medical-treatment cases.
required_elements: Count of DART cases (cases with days away, restricted work, or job transfer per the 300 log columns)
Total hours worked
200,000 base constant
failure_points: Confusing DART with DAFW/LTIR — DART includes restricted/transfer, lost-time (DAFW) does not
Not classifying a restricted-duty case as DART because 'no days were lost'
DART higher than TRIR (impossible — a data error)
notes: Return-to-work / light-duty programs are the primary DART lever: keeping an injured worker on restricted duty still counts as a DART case, but converting a would-be lost-time case to medical-only keeps it OUT of DART. This is also why aggressive RTW lowers EMR.
formula: DART = ( Number of DART cases × 200,000 ) ÷ Total hours worked
benchmarks: BLS SOII 2024: all private industry DART ≈ 1.4–1.5; Construction ≈ 1.5; Oil & gas extraction ≈ 0.4–0.9; Manufacturing ≈ 1.6–1.8. DART is roughly 55–65% of TRIR in most industries.

title: DAFW / LTIR — Days Away From Work (Lost Time) Rate
applicability: The narrowest severity rate: only cases with actual days away from work (lost-time), per 100 FTE. Sometimes labeled LTIR (Lost Time Incident Rate) or LTC rate. Excludes restricted-duty and transfer-only cases (which DART includes).
required_elements: Count of days-away cases (300 log column H)
Total hours worked
200,000 base constant
failure_points: Using DAFW and DART interchangeably
Excluding cases that had days away AND restricted days (still a DAFW case)
formula: DAFW/LTIR = ( Number of days-away cases × 200,000 ) ÷ Total hours worked
benchmarks: BLS SOII 2024: all private industry DAFW ≈ 0.8–0.9. Reported on the 300A as the 'cases with days away from work' column.

title: Severity Rate (Lost Workday Rate)
applicability: Measures how SERIOUS injuries are, not how often they occur: total lost/restricted days per 100 FTE. A company can have a low TRIR but a high severity rate if its few injuries are catastrophic. Not an OSHA-defined rate but widely required by owners.
required_elements: Total number of lost (and often restricted) workdays across all cases
Total hours worked
200,000 base constant
failure_points: Capping days at 180 for the rate when the client wants actual days (OSHA caps the 300-log count at 180 per case; confirm which the client wants)
Mixing lost days and restricted days without stating which are included
formula: Severity Rate = ( Total lost workdays × 200,000 ) ÷ Total hours worked

title: Fatality Rate & OSHA Reporting Triggers
applicability: Fatalities are reported to OSHA directly (not just logged) and, for benchmarking, expressed per 100,000 FTE from the BLS Census of Fatal Occupational Injuries (CFOI). Critical because fatality/severe-injury reporting failures are their own citation and a prequalification red flag.
required_elements: Report any work-related fatality to OSHA within 8 hours
Report any in-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye within 24 hours
Report by phone (1-800-321-OSHA), the nearest area office, or the online reporting form
Log the fatality on the OSHA 300 and retain the incident investigation
failure_points: Missing the 8-hour fatality / 24-hour hospitalization-amputation-eye reporting window
Reporting to the wrong channel or not documenting the report
No incident investigation on file to accompany the report
notes: Even one late severe-injury report can trigger an inspection and damage a prequalification score. The 8-hour / 24-hour rule is a frequent audit question.
formula:
Fatality Rate = ( Number of fatalities × 200,000 ) ÷ Total hours worked  (per-100-FTE basis)
BLS CFOI reports fatal injuries per 100,000 full-time-equivalent workers.
benchmarks: BLS CFOI: all-worker fatal injury rate ≈ 3.5 per 100,000 FTE; Construction ≈ 9.6; Oil & gas / mining ≈ 5–11; Agriculture ≈ 18–20; Transportation ≈ 13–14.

Named Insured — must exactly match the contracting legal entity (LLC vs. DBA vs. individual)
Insurer(s) affording coverage with NAIC # and A.M. Best rating (clients often require A- VII or better)
Each coverage line with policy number, effective/expiration dates, and limits (see individual coverage entries)
Description of Operations box — names the project and the required contractual wording
Certificate Holder — the hiring client / additional insured requesting the COI
Attached endorsement forms (AI, P&NC, WOS, notice of cancellation) — the COI checkboxes alone are not proof
failure_points: Named Insured on the COI doesn't match the contracting entity
COI shows 'additional insured' checked but the CG 20 10 / CG 20 37 endorsement is not attached
Coverage expired or lapses before the project completion / completed-operations tail
Carrier below the client's required A.M. Best rating
Limits below contract minimums; umbrella not shown as follow-form over GL and Auto

title: Commercial General Liability (CGL)
applicability: Third-party bodily injury and property damage coverage arising from the contractor's operations, products, and completed operations. The core line every hiring client requires. Written on the ISO CG 00 01 occurrence form (preferred over claims-made).
required_elements: Occurrence form (CG 00 01), not claims-made
Typical required limits: $1,000,000 per occurrence / $2,000,000 general aggregate / $2,000,000 products-completed operations aggregate / $1,000,000 personal & advertising injury
Products-Completed Operations coverage maintained through the required tail period
No exclusions that gut the coverage (e.g., action-over/employee-injury exclusion, residential, EIFS, height/exterior) where the work requires it
Aggregate applying per project/per location where required (CG 25 03 / CG 25 04)
failure_points: Limits below the $1M/$2M contract minimum
Claims-made form submitted where occurrence is required
Action-over (employee injury) exclusion present on energy/industrial work
Products-completed operations excluded or expired before the tail runs out
notes: CGL is the policy the AI, P&NC, and WOS endorsements attach to. When a client says 'name us as additional insured, primary & non-contributory, with waiver of subrogation,' they mean on the CGL (and usually Auto and Umbrella too).

title: Workers' Compensation & Employer's Liability
citation: State WC statute + ISO/NCCI WC policy
applicability: Statutory no-fault coverage for employee on-the-job injuries (Part One) plus Employer's Liability (Part Two) for injury claims that fall outside the WC statute. Mandatory in nearly every state for employers; the coverage behind the EMR.
required_elements: Part One — Workers' Compensation: statutory limits per the state(s) of operation
Part Two — Employer's Liability: typical required limits $1,000,000 each accident / $1,000,000 disease-policy limit / $1,000,000 disease-each employee
Correct states listed in Item 3.A. of the Information Page (all states where work is performed)
Waiver of Subrogation endorsement (WC 00 03 13) where the contract requires it
USL&H, Jones Act, or Voluntary Comp endorsements for maritime/offshore energy work where applicable
failure_points: State of operation missing from Item 3.A. (a gap in statutory coverage)
Employer's Liability limits below $1M/$1M/$1M
No WC 00 03 13 waiver of subrogation when required
Ghost/sole-proprietor policy excluding owners where the client requires owner coverage
Missing USL&H/Jones Act on offshore or dock work
notes: Additional-insured status does NOT apply to WC — the risk transfer here is the Waiver of Subrogation (WC 00 03 13). Certificate wording should carve WC out of the AI/P&NC language.

title: Commercial Automobile Liability
applicability: Bodily injury and property damage from owned, hired, and non-owned autos used in the business. Required for any contractor driving to/around a client site or hauling materials/equipment.
required_elements: 'Any Auto' or Owned + Hired + Non-Owned symbols covered
Typical required limit: $1,000,000 combined single limit (CSL)
Additional Insured endorsement (CA 20 48 designated insured) where required
Waiver of subrogation and primary/non-contributory where required
MCS-90 endorsement for DOT-regulated hazmat/interstate motor carriers (see FMCSA category)
failure_points: Hired & non-owned auto not covered though the contractor uses rentals/employee vehicles
Limit below $1M CSL
No MCS-90 where hazmat/interstate hauling requires it
Auto not added to the umbrella's underlying schedule

title: Umbrella / Excess Liability
citation: Follow-Form Umbrella over CGL / Auto / EL
applicability: Extra limits sitting above the CGL, Auto, and Employer's Liability underlying policies. Energy and heavy-industrial owners frequently require substantial umbrella limits on top of the $1M primary.
required_elements: Follow-form over CGL, Commercial Auto, and Employer's Liability (schedule of underlying)
Typical required limits: $1,000,000–$5,000,000+ (energy/petrochemical owners often require $5M–$25M total)
Additional insured and primary/non-contributory following form to the underlying
Drop-down / maintenance-of-underlying terms understood
failure_points: Umbrella not listing the required underlying policies (a coverage gap)
Total limits below the owner's required tower (e.g., $5M required, only $1M shown)
Umbrella not following form for AI/P&NC/WOS

title: Additional Insured Endorsement (AI)
applicability: Extends the contractor's CGL to cover the hiring client/owner as an insured for liability arising out of the contractor's work. Two forms are needed for a construction project's full lifecycle: ongoing operations AND completed operations. This is the single most-commonly-required risk-transfer endorsement.
required_elements: CG 20 10 — Additional Insured, Ongoing Operations (while the contractor is actively working)
CG 20 37 — Additional Insured, Products-Completed Operations (claims after the work is finished)
Schedule naming the client or 'as required by written contract'
Edition date awareness: on 04/13 and later forms, AI limits are the LESSER of the contract-required or the policy limits, and coverage is tied to the named insured's negligence
Blanket AI endorsement acceptable only if it names the party via written-contract trigger
failure_points: Only CG 20 10 provided — leaves completed-operations claims (the biggest construction losses) uncovered
COI shows AI but no endorsement page attached
Endorsement names the wrong legal entity or an expired policy
CG 20 37 references only ongoing operations language (doesn't reach 'your work' in the products-completed operations hazard)
notes: Require BOTH CG 20 10 and CG 20 37 in construction. 'My carrier can't issue CG 20 37' is false — all major carriers issue it, sometimes for a small fee.

title: Primary & Non-Contributory Endorsement (P&NC)
applicability: Makes the contractor's CGL pay FIRST ('primary') and stops the contractor's insurer from demanding the hiring client's own insurer share the loss ('non-contributory'). Paired with AI status so the client's own policy is never touched until the contractor's limits are exhausted.
required_elements: CG 20 01 (04 13 or later) attached to the CGL
Primary and non-contributory language present in the endorsement itself, not merely checked on the COI
Coordinated with the AI endorsement and, where required, on Auto and Umbrella
failure_points: P&NC only referenced on the certificate, not endorsed on the policy
AI granted without P&NC — leaves the client's carrier exposed to a contribution demand
P&NC missing on the umbrella so the tower isn't truly primary

title: Waiver of Subrogation (WOS)
applicability: The contractor's insurer waives its right to recover ('subrogate') from the hiring client after paying a claim. Required separately on the General Liability policy (CG 24 04) and the Workers' Compensation policy (WC 00 03 13) — they are different forms on different policies.
required_elements: CG 24 04 — Waiver of Transfer of Rights of Recovery, on the CGL
WC 00 03 13 — Waiver of Our Right to Recover From Others, on the Workers' Comp policy
Schedule naming the upstream party, or a blanket form triggered by a written waiver requirement
Waiver also on Auto/Umbrella where the contract requires it
failure_points: WC waiver omitted because the party assumed AI/GL waiver covers workers' comp (it does not)
Waiver only checked on the COI, endorsement not attached
Blanket waiver present but the contract required a scheduled (named) waiver

title: Notice of Cancellation Endorsement
applicability: Contractually required advance warning — typically 30 days (10 days for non-payment) — before the insurer cancels or non-renews, so the hiring client isn't blindsided by a lapse. Standard ACORD 25 language now only says notice will be given 'in accordance with the policy provisions,' so an actual endorsement is needed to bind a specific notice period to the certificate holder.
required_elements: Endorsement providing 30 days' advance written notice of cancellation/non-renewal to the certificate holder (10 days for non-payment)
Certificate holder named as the notice recipient
Applies across GL, Auto, WC, and Umbrella as required by contract
failure_points: Relying on the pre-printed ACORD 'endeavor to' language, which binds nothing
No endorsement actually naming the client as notice recipient
Notice period shorter than the contract requires

title: Incident Investigation & Reporting Program
applicability: All contractors. Prequal agencies require a written program governing how injuries, illnesses, near-misses and property-damage events are reported, investigated and closed out.
required_elements: Written procedure requiring prompt reporting of all incidents and near-misses, with no-reprisal language
Investigation methodology that identifies root cause (e.g., 5-Whys, cause tree) rather than only immediate cause
Defined timeline for starting and completing investigations
Corrective/preventive action tracking to closure with assigned owners and due dates
Roles and responsibilities (who reports, who investigates, management review)
OSHA recordkeeping/reporting triggers (fatality within 8 hours; inpatient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye within 24 hours)
Method to communicate lessons learned to the workforce
training: Supervisors and investigators trained in the investigation method and reporting timeline; all employees trained on how and when to report.
recordkeeping: Retain investigation reports, corrective-action logs, and OSHA 300/301 records per 1904 retention (5 years).
failure_points: Program stops at 'immediate cause' with no root-cause analysis
No corrective-action tracking to closure
Missing OSHA 8-hour / 24-hour reporting triggers
No near-miss reporting mechanism

title: Disciplinary & Enforcement Policy
citation: RAVS-required written program (OSHA General Duty Clause, 29 USC 654(a)(1))
applicability: All contractors. Prequal reviewers require a written, progressive policy showing safety rules are enforced consistently.
required_elements: Written progressive-discipline steps (e.g., verbal, written, suspension, termination) applied to safety-rule violations
Statement that the policy applies to all levels including supervisors and management
Provision for immediate action on willful or life-threatening violations
Consistent, documented application across the workforce
Employee acknowledgement of the policy
training: All employees informed of safety rules and the consequences of violations at orientation.
recordkeeping: Retain signed acknowledgements and disciplinary-action records.
failure_points: Policy exists but excludes supervisors/management
No progressive steps defined
No employee acknowledgement on file

title: Substance Abuse — Drug & Alcohol Program (non-DOT)
citation: RAVS-required written program (client-driven; distinct from 49 CFR Part 40 DOT testing)
applicability: Non-DOT-regulated workers. Most owner clients require a written substance-abuse policy covering the conditions under which testing occurs.
required_elements: Written policy prohibiting drug/alcohol use, possession, and impairment on the job
Testing conditions covered: pre-employment, reasonable suspicion, post-incident, random, return-to-duty
Defined consequences of a positive test and of refusal to test
Chain-of-custody and confidentiality provisions
Compliance with applicable state law and, where workers are safety-sensitive, alignment with DOT 49 CFR Part 40 procedures
Employee Assistance Program (EAP) or referral information where offered
training: Supervisors trained to recognize reasonable-suspicion indicators; employees informed of the policy at hire.
recordkeeping: Retain signed policy acknowledgements and testing records per applicable law; keep DOT and non-DOT records separate.
failure_points: No post-incident or reasonable-suspicion testing defined
Silent on refusal-to-test consequences
Conflicts with state law (e.g., marijuana provisions)

title: Behavior-Based Safety / Safety Observation Program
applicability: Contractors on sites that require a proactive observation/leading-indicator program.
required_elements: Written process for peer safety observations of at-risk vs. safe behaviors
A defined observation card/checklist and how data is collected
Feedback loop: how observations are reviewed and acted on
Tracking of leading indicators and trend review by management
No-blame, coaching-based approach
training: Observers trained on the observation process and giving effective feedback.
recordkeeping: Retain observation records and trend analyses.
failure_points: Data collected but never analyzed or acted on
Used punitively instead of for coaching

title: Management of Change (MOC) Program
applicability: Facilities/operations where changes to process, equipment, chemicals, procedures, or personnel can introduce new hazards. Required under PSM and commonly required by owner clients beyond PSM scope.
required_elements: Written procedure to review changes to technology, equipment, procedures, and organization before implementation
Hazard/technical basis review of the proposed change
Authorization/approval requirements before the change is made
Update of affected process safety information, procedures, and drawings
Communication and training of affected employees and contractors on the change
Distinction between temporary and permanent changes with time limits on temporary changes
training: Employees and contractors affected by a change trained prior to startup.
recordkeeping: Retain MOC review, approval, and close-out records.
failure_points: Only covers equipment, not procedural or organizational change
No pre-startup review or approval step
Temporary changes never closed out

title: Contractor / Subcontractor Safety Management Program
applicability: Contractors that hire lower-tier subcontractors, and host employers evaluating contractors.
required_elements: Written process to pre-qualify subcontractors on safety performance (EMR, TRIR, programs)
Communication of site hazards and rules to subcontractors
Verification of subcontractor training and insurance
Oversight/auditing of subcontractor work and enforcement of safety rules
Evaluation of subcontractor performance and re-qualification
training: Subcontractor employees receive site-specific orientation before starting work.
recordkeeping: Retain prequalification records, orientation rosters, and performance evaluations.
failure_points: No documented prequalification criteria
No verification of sub training/insurance
No performance evaluation loop

title: New Employee Safety Orientation & Training Program
citation: 29 CFR 1910 Subpart-wide training duties + RAVS-required written program
applicability: All contractors. Prequal reviewers require a documented orientation covering hazards and programs before work begins.
required_elements: Written orientation curriculum covering company safety rules, hazard communication, PPE, emergency procedures, and incident reporting
Site-specific hazard orientation for each new location
Documentation of completion (signed roster/acknowledgement) before the employee starts work
Competency verification appropriate to the job
Refresher/annual training schedule
training: This program IS the training baseline; identifies who delivers it and how competency is confirmed.
recordkeeping: Retain signed orientation records and a training matrix by employee and topic.
failure_points: No proof of completion before work starts
Generic only, with no site-specific component
No training matrix showing who is trained on what

title: Job Safety Analysis (JSA/JHA) & Hazard Identification Program
applicability: All contractors. A written process for identifying task hazards and controls before work.
required_elements: Written procedure to break jobs into steps, identify the hazard of each step, and define controls
Use of the hierarchy of controls (elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE)
Requirement to perform/review a JSA before non-routine or high-risk tasks
Worker participation in developing and reviewing JSAs
Method to update JSAs when conditions or steps change
training: Supervisors and crews trained to develop, use, and review JSAs.
recordkeeping: Retain completed JSAs for representative and high-risk tasks.
failure_points: JSAs are generic and not task/site-specific
Controls listed do not follow the hierarchy of controls
No worker involvement

title: Hand & Portable Power Tools Safety Program
applicability: Contractors whose employees use hand tools and portable powered tools.
required_elements: Written safe-use, inspection, and maintenance requirements for hand and power tools
Guarding requirements for point-of-operation, rotating parts, and moving parts
Removal-from-service criteria for damaged or defective tools
PPE requirements associated with tool use
Prohibition on compressed air >30 psi for cleaning unless proper controls are used
training: Employees trained on safe use, inspection, and hazards of the specific tools they use.
recordkeeping: Retain tool inspection and defective-tool removal records where used.
failure_points: No inspection / remove-from-service criteria
Guarding requirements omitted

title: Heat Illness Prevention Program
citation: OSHA General Duty Clause 29 USC 654(a)(1) + OSHA Heat NEP (client-required written program)
applicability: Contractors with outdoor or hot indoor work. Increasingly required by owner clients and the subject of OSHA's Heat National Emphasis Program and pending rulemaking.
required_elements: Written plan providing access to water, shade/cooling, and rest breaks
Acclimatization schedule for new and returning workers
Heat-index/trigger thresholds that increase protective measures
Symptom recognition and emergency response procedures for heat illness
Designation of a person responsible for monitoring conditions
training: Workers and supervisors trained to recognize heat-illness signs and the plan's controls.
recordkeeping: Retain training records and any heat-related incident records.
failure_points: No acclimatization provisions for new workers
No defined heat triggers
No emergency response for heat illness

title: Fire Prevention & Protection Program (Construction)
applicability: Construction contractors. Written firefighting/prevention program for the jobsite.
required_elements: Firefighting equipment provided, conspicuously located, and maintained (extinguishers rated and inspected)
Fire-extinguisher distribution meeting the required travel-distance/area ratios
Control of flammable/combustible material storage and ignition sources
Fire alarm/notification and site emergency response procedures
Inspection and maintenance schedule for fire equipment
training: Employees expected to use extinguishers trained on their use; all employees trained on site fire procedures.
recordkeeping: Retain monthly extinguisher inspection records and annual maintenance.
failure_points: Extinguishers not inspected monthly / not annually maintained
Insufficient extinguisher coverage for the site area

title: Machine Guarding Program
applicability: Contractors operating machinery with points of operation, rotating parts, or in-going nip points.
required_elements: Written program identifying machines requiring guards and the guarding method for each hazard
Point-of-operation guarding that meets the standard for each machine
Anchoring of fixed machinery to prevent walking/moving
Guard inspection and maintenance requirements
Integration with lockout/tagout for guard removal during service
training: Operators trained on machine hazards, guards, and safe operation.
recordkeeping: Retain machine hazard assessments and guard inspection records.
failure_points: Point-of-operation left unguarded
No link to LOTO when guards are removed

title: Compressed Gas Cylinder Safety Program
applicability: Contractors that store, handle, or use compressed gas cylinders (welding, oilfield, industrial).
required_elements: Written storage requirements: upright, secured/chained, valve caps in place, oxidizers separated from fuel gases by distance or barrier
Handling and transport procedures (no lifting by valve cap, cylinders moved with valve protection)
Inspection of cylinders and regulators before use
Separation of full and empty cylinders and proper labeling
training: Employees trained on safe storage, handling, and use of cylinders.
recordkeeping: Retain inspection records where required.
failure_points: Oxygen and fuel-gas cylinders stored together without the required separation
Cylinders unsecured or stored without valve caps

title: Motor Vehicle / Fleet Safety Program
citation: RAVS-required written program (OSHA General Duty Clause; NHTSA/FMCSA where applicable)
applicability: Contractors whose employees drive company or personal vehicles for work (non-CMV fleet safety; complements DOT programs for CMV drivers).
required_elements: Written driver eligibility and Motor Vehicle Record (MVR) review criteria
Seatbelt, distracted-driving (cell phone), and impairment prohibitions
Vehicle inspection and maintenance requirements
Journey management / trip-planning for high-risk or long drives
Accident reporting and investigation procedures
training: Drivers oriented on the policy; defensive-driving where required by client.
recordkeeping: Retain MVR reviews, vehicle inspection logs, and incident records.
failure_points: No MVR review / driver eligibility criteria
Silent on distracted driving

title: Fitness for Duty Program
applicability: Contractors on sites requiring assurance that workers are physically and mentally able to perform safety-sensitive tasks.
required_elements: Written criteria for physical/medical ability to perform assigned safety-sensitive work
Process for post-injury/illness return-to-work evaluation
Fatigue-management provisions where extended shifts occur
Confidential handling of medical information consistent with ADA/HIPAA
Referral process when an employee is not fit for duty
training: Supervisors trained to recognize and respond to fitness-for-duty concerns.
recordkeeping: Retain fitness-for-duty and return-to-work records confidentially.
failure_points: No return-to-work evaluation process
Medical information not handled confidentially

title: Walking-Working Surfaces & Fall Protection (General Industry)
applicability: General-industry workplaces with elevated surfaces, holes, stairways, ladders, or fall hazards of 4 feet or more.
required_elements: Fall protection where a fall hazard of 4 ft or more exists (guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection system)
Inspection and maintenance of walking-working surfaces in a clean, orderly, dry condition
Ladder condition and use requirements; fixed-ladder fall protection phase-in for ladders over 24 ft
Selection and use criteria for personal fall protection systems (1910.140)
Written procedures where rope descent systems or designated areas are used
training: Employees trained under 1910.30 on fall hazards, fall-protection systems, and equipment before exposure; retrain when needed.
recordkeeping: Retain 1910.30 training certification (employee, date, trainer).
failure_points: Using the 6-ft construction trigger instead of the 4-ft GI trigger
No 1910.30 training certification
Fixed-ladder fall-protection phase-in ignored

title: Portable Fire Extinguishers
applicability: Employers that provide portable fire extinguishers for employee use. If a total evacuation policy applies instead, 1910.157 use/training provisions may not.
required_elements: Extinguishers selected, provided, and mounted so they are accessible without exposing employees to injury
Monthly visual inspection and annual maintenance check
Hydrostatic testing at required intervals by extinguisher type
Placement meeting maximum travel-distance requirements by hazard class
If employees are expected to use extinguishers, an educational program on their use and the hazards of incipient-stage firefighting
training: Employees expected to use extinguishers trained upon initial assignment and annually thereafter.
recordkeeping: Record monthly inspections (retain 1 year) and annual maintenance; document hydrostatic tests.
failure_points: No monthly inspection record
No annual training where employees are expected to use extinguishers
Extinguishers exceed required travel distance

title: Medical Services & First Aid
applicability: All general-industry employers; heightened where the worksite is not in near proximity to an infirmary, clinic, or hospital.
required_elements: Provision for prompt medical attention; where no infirmary/clinic/hospital is in near proximity, a person adequately trained to render first aid
Adequate first-aid supplies readily available
Where employees may be exposed to corrosive materials, suitable facilities for quick drenching/flushing of eyes and body within the work area
Coordination with the Bloodborne Pathogens exposure control plan for responders
training: First-aid/CPR trained responders where required by proximity; refresher per certifying body.
recordkeeping: Retain first-aid/CPR certifications and eyewash inspection records.
failure_points: No trained first-aider where a hospital is not nearby
Eyewash/drench facilities missing where corrosives are used

title: Electric Power Generation, Transmission & Distribution
applicability: Operation and maintenance of electric power generation, transmission, and distribution installations (utility and utility-contractor work).
required_elements: Written safety-related work practices and an electrical hazard-assessment for the tasks performed
Minimum approach distances and energized-work procedures; job briefings before each job
Arc-flash hazard assessment and provision of arc-rated protective clothing/PPE
Host/contract-employer information exchange on hazards and conditions
Enclosed-space and confined-space entry procedures where applicable
Lockout/tagout and system-operator coordination for de-energized work
training: Qualified/unqualified employee training on the work practices, hazards, and emergency procedures (including pole-top/bucket rescue and CPR).
recordkeeping: Retain training records, job briefings where documented, and PPE/electrical-equipment test records.
failure_points: No arc-flash assessment / arc-rated PPE
No host-contractor information exchange
Missing pole-top/CPR rescue training

title: Cranes, Derricks, Hoists & Slings (General Industry Rigging)
applicability: General-industry use of overhead/gantry cranes, crawler/truck/locomotive cranes, and slings for material handling.
required_elements: Rated-load markings and load-limit compliance; no loading beyond rated capacity
Frequent and periodic documented inspections of cranes, hoists, and rigging
Sling inspection each shift and removal-from-service criteria for damaged slings
Operator qualification and safe-operating procedures (no side loading, proper hitching)
Maintenance and repair program for lifting equipment
training: Operators and riggers trained on safe operation, inspection, and load handling.
recordkeeping: Retain periodic crane inspection records and sling/hoist inspection logs.
failure_points: No documented periodic crane inspections
Damaged slings not removed from service
Operators not qualified

title: Flammable Liquids
applicability: Storage, handling, and use of flammable and combustible liquids in general industry.
required_elements: Storage quantity limits, approved containers, and flammable-liquid storage cabinets/rooms per class
Bonding and grounding during transfer of flammable liquids
Ignition-source control in storage/handling areas
Ventilation and spill-control provisions
Coordination with Hazard Communication and, where applicable, SPCC
training: Employees trained on safe handling, transfer, and storage of flammable liquids and the associated hazards.
recordkeeping: Retain inspection records for storage areas and cabinets where used.
failure_points: Exceeding container/cabinet quantity limits
No bonding/grounding during transfer
Ignition sources near storage

title: Ionizing Radiation
applicability: Workplaces using sources of ionizing radiation (e.g., industrial radiography, gauges). NRC/Agreement-State licensing may also apply.
required_elements: Surveys and monitoring to evaluate radiation hazards
Personnel dosimetry where doses may exceed the required fraction of limits
Restricted-area posting, caution signs, and access control
Dose limits for occupational exposure and for restricted areas
Notification, reporting, and record requirements for exposures
training: Workers instructed on radiation hazards, protective measures, and applicable regulations.
recordkeeping: Retain radiation survey, monitoring, and dose records per the standard.
failure_points: No dosimetry where required
Restricted areas not posted
Exposure records not maintained

title: Personal Protective Equipment (Construction)
applicability: Construction employers whose employees are exposed to hazards requiring head, eye/face, hearing, foot, hand, or respiratory protection.
required_elements: Hazard assessment identifying required PPE by task
Head protection (hard hats) where overhead/impact/electrical hazards exist
Eye and face protection appropriate to the hazard
Hearing protection where noise exposures require it; respiratory protection per 1926.103/1910.134
Employer-provided PPE at no cost (with limited exceptions) and training on use, care, and limitations
training: Employees trained on when PPE is necessary, what to use, and how to don/doff, adjust, and maintain it.
recordkeeping: Retain the hazard assessment and PPE training records.
failure_points: No documented hazard assessment
PPE not provided at no cost where required
No training on PPE use

title: Welding, Cutting & Brazing / Hot Work (Construction)
applicability: Construction operations involving gas/arc welding, cutting, and other hot work.
required_elements: Hot-work permit system and fire-watch requirements before, during, and after hot work
Removal or protection of combustibles within the fire-hazard radius
Compressed-gas cylinder storage, handling, and use requirements
Ventilation and respiratory protection for welding fumes/gases
Fire-extinguishing equipment available at the hot-work area
training: Welders and fire watches trained on hot-work hazards, permits, and fire-watch duties.
recordkeeping: Retain hot-work permits and equipment inspection records.
failure_points: No fire watch / no post-work monitoring period
Combustibles not cleared or protected
Cylinders stored improperly

title: Electrical Safety (Construction)
applicability: Construction work involving electrical installations, temporary wiring, and work on or near energized parts.
required_elements: Ground-fault protection: GFCI or an Assured Equipment Grounding Conductor Program for temporary power
Safe clearance/approach distances from energized lines and equipment
Lockout/tagout and de-energization before work where feasible
Guarding of live parts and proper use of flexible cords/assured grounding
Only qualified persons work on or near exposed energized parts
training: Qualified and affected employees trained on electrical hazards and safe work practices.
recordkeeping: Retain the Assured Equipment Grounding Conductor Program records and equipment tests.
failure_points: No GFCI and no AEGCP for temporary power
Unqualified workers near energized parts
Damaged cords in service

title: Concrete & Masonry Construction
applicability: Construction involving cast-in-place concrete, formwork, shoring, precast, and masonry walls.
required_elements: Formwork designed, fabricated, erected, and shored to support all loads; shoring/reshoring per drawings
No loading of concrete structures until they can support the loads (adequate strength confirmed)
Limited-access zone for masonry-wall construction and bracing of walls over 8 ft until permanently supported
Protection from protruding reinforcing steel (impalement)
Inspection of equipment and tools (e.g., no removal of formwork until strength verified)
training: Workers trained on formwork/shoring, masonry-wall hazards, and the limited-access zone.
recordkeeping: Retain formwork/shoring drawings and inspections where required.
failure_points: No limited-access zone during masonry work
Unbraced walls over 8 ft
Exposed rebar not protected against impalement

title: Blasting & Use of Explosives (Construction)
applicability: Construction operations that store, handle, transport, or use explosives and conduct blasting.
required_elements: Only authorized, qualified blasters conduct blasting operations
Written procedures for handling, transporting, and storing explosives (magazines, separation of explosives and detonators)
Blasting-area security: warning signals, guarding, and clearing personnel before firing
Prohibition on blasting near energized power/radio sources unless controlled
Post-blast inspection procedures and misfire handling
training: Blasters qualified per state/local requirements; crews trained on blast-area security and signals.
recordkeeping: Retain explosives inventory/magazine records and blast logs.
failure_points: Unqualified blaster
Explosives and detonators stored together
No blast-area security/warning procedure

title: Power Transmission & Distribution (Construction)
applicability: Construction of electric transmission and distribution lines and equipment.
required_elements: Job briefings covering hazards, procedures, and PPE before each job
Minimum approach distances and energized-line work procedures
Arc-flash hazard assessment and arc-rated clothing/PPE
Grounding of de-energized lines and equipment before work
Host/contract-employer information exchange (aligns with 1910.269)
training: Employees trained on the work practices, minimum approach distances, and emergency/rescue procedures.
recordkeeping: Retain training, job-briefing (where documented), and grounding/test records.
failure_points: No arc-flash assessment
De-energized lines not grounded before work
No job briefing

title: Occupational Noise Exposure (Construction)
applicability: Construction work where employee noise exposure equals or exceeds the permissible levels.
required_elements: Feasible administrative or engineering controls to reduce noise
Hearing protection provided and used where controls are insufficient
Exposure evaluation against the 90 dBA 8-hour permissible level (and action-level considerations)
A continuing, effective hearing conservation program where exposures warrant it
training: Workers informed on noise hazards and the use of hearing protection.
recordkeeping: Retain noise-exposure measurements and any audiometric records where a program is in place.
failure_points: No engineering/administrative controls attempted
Hearing protection available but not enforced
No exposure evaluation

title: Dropped Objects Prevention Program
citation: Client-required (OSHA General Duty Clause 29 USC 654(a)(1); ANSI/ISEA 121)
applicability: Work at heights or below overhead work (oil & gas, construction, industrial). Very common on operator requirement lists.
required_elements: Written program to identify and control static and dynamic dropped-object hazards
Tool tethering/securing at height and use of tool bags/containers per ANSI/ISEA 121
Barricading and exclusion zones below overhead work
Inspection of tethers, anchors, and securing devices before use
Requirement to secure loose items (bolts, small tools) when working at height
training: Workers trained on dropped-object hazards, tethering methods, and exclusion zones.
recordkeeping: Retain tethering-equipment inspections and training records.
failure_points: No tool-tethering requirement at height
No exclusion/drop zones below overhead work

title: Line of Fire / Body Positioning Program
applicability: Tasks with stored energy, pinch points, pressurized systems, suspended loads, or moving equipment. Standard operator requirement in energy and construction.
required_elements: Written program defining line-of-fire hazard categories (caught-between, struck-by, pinch points, stored energy, pressure release)
Requirement to identify line-of-fire exposures during JSA/pre-job planning
Body-positioning rules to keep workers out of the line of fire (no hands-in-line-of-fire, stand clear of suspended loads/hoses under pressure)
Controls for released energy (whip checks on hoses, restraint of stored energy)
Stop-work expectation when a person enters the line of fire
training: Workers trained to recognize and position themselves out of the line of fire.
recordkeeping: Retain training records and JSAs documenting line-of-fire controls.
failure_points: Program is generic with no task-specific line-of-fire categories
No hose/pressure release controls (whip checks)

title: Hand & Finger Safety Program
citation: Client-required (OSHA General Duty Clause; 29 CFR 1910.138 hand protection)
applicability: Any manual work; hand injuries are the leading recordable in many trades, so operators frequently require a dedicated program.
required_elements: Hand-hazard assessment by task and glove selection matched to the hazard (cut, chemical, impact, heat)
Pinch-point and line-of-fire awareness for hands
Prohibition on removing machine guards and on hands-in-line-of-fire practices
Impact-glove requirements where struck/pinch hazards exist
Injury-trend review focused on hand/finger incidents
training: Workers trained on hand hazards, correct glove selection, and safe hand placement.
recordkeeping: Retain the glove-selection assessment and training records.
failure_points: Glove selection not matched to the hazard (cut level, chemical)
No pinch-point/line-of-fire component

title: Ergonomics / Manual Material Handling Program
citation: Client-required (OSHA General Duty Clause 29 USC 654(a)(1); NIOSH lifting guidance)
applicability: Work involving lifting, repetitive motion, awkward postures, or manual material handling.
required_elements: Written process to identify ergonomic risk factors (force, repetition, posture, vibration)
Manual-handling controls: mechanical aids, team lifts, weight limits, job rotation
Workstation/tool design guidance to reduce strain
Early reporting process for musculoskeletal discomfort and a response procedure
Periodic review of ergonomic injury trends
training: Workers trained on safe lifting, manual-handling techniques, and early symptom reporting.
recordkeeping: Retain ergonomic assessments and MSD injury-trend records.
failure_points: No risk-factor assessment
No early-reporting mechanism for MSDs

title: Infectious Disease / Pandemic Preparedness Program
citation: Client-required (OSHA General Duty Clause; CDC/OSHA guidance; 29 CFR 1910.1030 where blood/OPIM)
applicability: Workforces needing continuity and exposure control during outbreaks; commonly requested since 2020 and in healthcare-adjacent work.
required_elements: Written plan for exposure assessment and controls during an infectious-disease event
Hierarchy of controls: engineering (ventilation), administrative (distancing, screening), and PPE (respirators where needed per 1910.134)
Hygiene, disinfection, and case-response/return-to-work procedures
Business-continuity provisions and communication plan
Coordination with the Bloodborne Pathogens plan where blood/OPIM exposure exists
training: Workers trained on transmission, hygiene, PPE, and reporting during an event.
recordkeeping: Retain the plan, training records, and any exposure/case records confidentially.
failure_points: No hierarchy of controls
Respirator use without a 1910.134 program
