title: Injury & Illness Prevention Program (Cal/OSHA IIPP)
citation: 8 CCR 3203 (California Code of Regulations, Title 8) — MANDATORY in California
applicability: REQUIRED for every employer with operations in California (and analogous 'safety program' rules in several other state-plan states). A frequent hard-fail if missing.
required_elements: Identification of the person(s) with authority and responsibility for the program
A system for ensuring employees comply with safe work practices (including recognition/discipline)
A system for communicating with employees on health & safety (meetings, training, a way to report hazards anonymously)
Procedures for identifying and evaluating workplace hazards (scheduled inspections)
Procedures to investigate occupational injury/illness
Methods/procedures for correcting unsafe conditions in a timely manner
Training program (general and job-specific)
Recordkeeping of inspections and training
training: Employees trained when the program is established, on new hire, on new assignments/hazards, and when new hazards are introduced.
recordkeeping: Retain records of scheduled/periodic inspections (identifier, date, action) and training (name, date, topic); retention per 8 CCR 3203.
failure_points: Using a generic federal EAP in place of a compliant IIPP for CA operations
No hazard-assessment inspection schedule
No documented communication system

title: Heat Illness Prevention (Cal/OSHA)
applicability: California outdoor places of employment (and, under 3396, most indoor workplaces reaching 82°F). Stricter and more prescriptive than the federal general-duty approach.
required_elements: Provision of fresh, pure, suitably cool drinking water (1 quart/employee/hour)
Access to shade at or below 80°F outdoors, with high-heat procedures at/above 95°F
Written acclimatization procedures for new/returning employees and during heat waves
Emergency response procedures for heat-illness symptoms
For indoor (3396): assessment at 82°F, cool-down areas, and control measures at 87°F (or 82°F for radiant-heat/clothing conditions)
training: Employees and supervisors trained on heat-illness risk factors, prevention, water/shade/rest, and emergency response.
recordkeeping: Retain the written plan and training records; document high-heat procedures.
failure_points: Using a generic federal heat plan for CA work
No high-heat (95°F) procedures
No indoor-heat plan where 3396 applies

title: Workplace Violence Prevention Program
citation: CA SB 553 / Labor Code 6401.9 (general industry) & 8 CCR 3342 (healthcare); OSHA General Duty Clause elsewhere
applicability: MANDATORY for most California employers (SB 553, effective 2024) and California healthcare (3342); increasingly requested by clients nationally.
required_elements: Written plan with names/titles responsible for implementation
Procedures for employee involvement in developing and implementing the plan
Procedures to accept and respond to reports of workplace violence, with no retaliation
Procedures to identify, evaluate, and correct workplace-violence hazards
A violent-incident log recording each incident
Post-incident response and investigation procedures
training: Initial and annual training on the plan, hazards, reporting, and response.
recordkeeping: Maintain the violent-incident log (5 yrs), training records (1 yr), and hazard-ID/correction records (5 yrs) per SB 553.
failure_points: No violent-incident log
No annual training
Plan not specific to the workplace's hazards

title: Fatigue Management Program
citation: Client-required (OSHA General Duty Clause; API RP 755 for refining/petrochemical)
applicability: Extended-hours, shift, and safety-sensitive operations (energy, refining, 24/7 sites). API RP 755 is commonly required by operators.
required_elements: Written hours-of-service limits and maximum shift/consecutive-day thresholds
Shift-scheduling design to manage cumulative fatigue and night work
Fatigue hazard identification and mitigation (rest breaks, napping policy where used)
Training on sleep, fatigue, and personal risk factors
Process to address fatigue-related incidents
training: Workers and supervisors trained on recognizing and managing fatigue.
recordkeeping: Retain hours-worked records and fatigue-training records.
failure_points: No maximum hours/consecutive-day limits
No shift-design controls for night work

title: Cold Stress / Cold Weather Work Program
citation: Client-required (OSHA General Duty Clause 29 USC 654(a)(1); NIOSH cold-stress guidance)
applicability: Outdoor or cold-environment work (northern operations, winter construction, refrigerated spaces).
required_elements: Written procedures for cold-stress hazard recognition (hypothermia, frostbite, trench foot)
Engineering/administrative controls: warming areas, work/rest schedules, wind-chill thresholds
Cold-weather PPE and layered-clothing guidance
Emergency response for cold-stress illness
Monitoring of conditions and a responsible person
training: Workers trained to recognize and respond to cold-stress conditions.
recordkeeping: Retain training and any cold-stress incident records.
failure_points: No wind-chill/work-rest thresholds
No warming areas provided

title: Combustible Dust Program
citation: OSHA Combustible Dust NEP (CPL 03-00-008) + NFPA 652/654; 29 CFR 1910.22/.307/.1200
applicability: Facilities that generate combustible dusts (grain, wood, metal, plastics, food, chemicals). Subject of an OSHA National Emphasis Program.
required_elements: Dust Hazard Analysis (DHA) identifying combustible-dust hazards per NFPA 652
Housekeeping program to control dust accumulation (limits on layer depth)
Ignition-source control and proper electrical classification in dust areas
Engineering controls (dust collection, explosion venting/suppression) where warranted
Hazard communication for combustible-dust hazards
training: Employees trained on combustible-dust hazards, housekeeping, and ignition control.
recordkeeping: Retain the DHA, housekeeping logs, and equipment inspections.
failure_points: No Dust Hazard Analysis
Dust accumulation exceeds safe layer depth
Non-classified electrical equipment in dust areas

title: Traffic Control / Work Zone & Flagger Safety Program
applicability: Roadway, roadside, or mobile-equipment work zones; utility and construction work near traffic.
required_elements: Traffic Control Plan (TCP) for the work zone consistent with the MUTCD
Proper signs, signals, barricades, and channelizing devices
Flagger procedures and high-visibility apparel (ANSI/ISEA 107) for exposed workers
Flagger training/certification where required by state/agency
Internal traffic control for mobile equipment and spotters
training: Flaggers trained/certified; workers trained on the work-zone plan and high-visibility requirements.
recordkeeping: Retain flagger certifications and the traffic control plan.
failure_points: No MUTCD-consistent traffic control plan
Untrained flaggers
No high-visibility apparel

title: Rigging, Lifting & Signalperson Program
applicability: Crane-supported lifts and rigging operations in construction; complements the crane standard.
required_elements: Qualified rigger and qualified signalperson requirements for applicable lifts
Rigging (sling/hardware) inspection before use and removal-from-service criteria
Lift planning for critical/complex lifts (load weight, capacity, configuration)
Standard hand/voice signals and exclusive signal communication
Barricading of the swing radius and load path; no workers under suspended loads
training: Riggers and signalpersons qualified per 1926.1400 Subpart CC; crews trained on lift plans.
recordkeeping: Retain rigger/signalperson qualifications, rigging inspections, and critical-lift plans.
failure_points: Unqualified rigger/signalperson
No critical-lift plan
Workers under suspended loads

title: Housekeeping & Material Storage Program
applicability: All worksites; poor housekeeping is a common audit finding and a driver of slips/trips and fire hazards.
required_elements: Written housekeeping standards keeping walking-working surfaces clean, dry, and orderly
Safe material storage: stable stacking, height limits, aisle/egress clearance, and load ratings
Regular removal of scrap, waste, and combustibles; container/labeling requirements
Trip-hazard and spill control procedures
Housekeeping inspections and accountability
training: Workers trained on housekeeping standards and safe storage/stacking.
recordkeeping: Retain housekeeping inspection records.
failure_points: Blocked egress/aisles
Unstable/over-height storage
Accumulated combustibles

title: Confined and Enclosed Spaces — Shipyard (Competent Person / Marine Chemist)
applicability: Shipyard employment — ship repair, shipbuilding, shipbreaking, and related work in confined or enclosed spaces aboard vessels or in landside structures.
required_elements: Designation of a Competent Person to test and inspect confined/enclosed spaces before and during entry
Marine Chemist or Certified Industrial Hygiene certificate ('Safe for Workers'/'Safe for Hot Work') where required
Atmospheric testing for oxygen, flammable vapors (LEL), and toxic contaminants before entry and periodically
Labeling/posting of space status and controls to prevent unauthorized entry
Ventilation and continuous monitoring procedures for spaces immediately dangerous to life or health (IDLH)
Rescue and emergency procedures with equipment and trained standby personnel
training: Competent Person training; employee training on space hazards, testing results, PPE, and rescue. Retraining when conditions change.
recordkeeping: Retain Competent Person test records and Marine Chemist certificates for the duration of the job/shift as required by 1915.7.
failure_points: No designated Competent Person or Marine Chemist certificate for hot work
Atmospheric testing not repeated as conditions change
Rescue plan not space-specific or standby not equipped

title: Fire Protection in Shipyard Employment
applicability: All shipyard employment — establishes the fire safety program for ship repair, shipbuilding, and shipbreaking, including hot work and fire watch requirements.
required_elements: Written Fire Safety Plan per 1915.502: responsibilities, hot work permits, fire watch, alarm/notification, evacuation, and coordination with the fire response organization
Designation of a Fire Watch and their duties during and after hot work
Hot work authorization and control by a Competent Person
Fire response organization (in-house brigade or outside department) with defined capabilities
Employee alarm and notification system and evacuation procedures
Inspection and maintenance of fire detection, alarm, and suppression equipment
training: Training for fire watches, hot work operators, and members of the fire response organization; annual review.
recordkeeping: Retain the written fire safety plan, hot work permits, and fire watch/inspection records.
failure_points: No written fire safety plan or fire response organization identified
Fire watch not posted or not maintained 30 minutes after hot work
Hot work not authorized by a Competent Person

title: Personal Protective Equipment — Shipyard Employment
applicability: Shipyard employment where employees are exposed to hazards requiring PPE, including fall protection, respiratory protection, and personal fall arrest in shipyards.
required_elements: Written hazard assessment certifying the PPE required for each task
Selection, provision, and maintenance of head, eye, face, foot, hand, and body protection
Personal fall arrest and positioning systems where required (1915.159/.160)
Employer-provided PPE at no cost, with fit and condition verified
Employee training on use, limitations, care, and disposal of PPE
training: Training so each employee knows when PPE is necessary, what type, how to don/doff, limitations, and proper care.
recordkeeping: Retain the written PPE hazard-assessment certification and training records.
failure_points: No written hazard assessment certification
Fall protection not provided for shipyard elevations
PPE not provided at no cost or not maintained

title: Marine Terminals — Safety and Health Program
applicability: Employment within marine terminals, including cargo handling and related activities at waterfront facilities (loading, unloading, movement, and storage of cargo).
required_elements: Accident prevention program and hazard controls for terminal operations
Cargo handling gear inspection, testing, and certification program (1917.50)
Powered industrial truck and material handling equipment safety
Container and Ro-Ro operations procedures where applicable
First aid, emergency action, and injury reporting procedures
training: Employee training on terminal hazards, equipment operation, and emergency procedures.
recordkeeping: Retain gear certification, equipment inspection, and injury records.
failure_points: Cargo handling gear not certificated/tested
No accident prevention program
Untrained equipment operators

title: Longshoring — Safety and Health Program
applicability: Longshoring operations — loading, unloading, moving, or handling cargo aboard vessels or between vessel and shore.
required_elements: Accident prevention and hazard control procedures aboard vessels
Gear certification and inspection for cargo handling equipment
Fall protection, access, and gangway/ladder safety
Atmospheric testing for enclosed cargo spaces and fumigated cargo
First aid, life-saving, and emergency response equipment and procedures
training: Qualified/designated person training for cargo gear and hazardous operations; employee hazard training.
recordkeeping: Retain gear certification and inspection records and injury reports.
failure_points: Cargo gear not certificated
No atmospheric testing for fumigated/enclosed cargo
Inadequate access/fall protection to vessels

title: Telecommunications
applicability: Work on, or associated with, telecommunications lines, cables, equipment, central offices, and outside plant (aerial and underground), including installation and maintenance.
required_elements: Employee training and qualification for the tasks and hazards (aerial, underground, central office)
Personal protective equipment and personal fall arrest / body-belt use for climbing and aerial work
Approach distances and procedures near energized power conductors
Manhole and unvented vault entry: testing, ventilation, and attendant procedures
Cable fault locating, tree trimming, and derrick/aerial-lift truck procedures
Grounding and protection against buried/aerial cable hazards
training: Task- and hazard-specific training; first-aid/CPR for designated employees; pole-climbing qualification.
recordkeeping: Retain training and qualification records; equipment inspection logs.
failure_points: No pole-climbing/aerial qualification records
Manhole entry without atmospheric testing/ventilation
Approach distances to power conductors not defined

title: Logging Operations
applicability: All logging operations regardless of end use of the wood — felling, bucking, limbing, yarding, loading, and transport of trees/logs.
required_elements: First-aid and CPR training for each employee, with first-aid kits at the worksite and each vehicle
PPE: head, eye, leg (chain-saw chaps), foot (cut-resistant), and hand protection provided at no cost
Chain saw and machine operation safe practices, inspection, and maintenance
Safe work procedures for felling, limbing, bucking, and manual/mechanical yarding
Signaling and communication among crew; safe distances (two-tree-length rule)
Danger-tree and environmental hazard evaluation before work begins
training: Initial and as-needed training on safe operation of each machine/tool; first-aid/CPR current; documented competency before solo work.
recordkeeping: Retain training certifications and first-aid/CPR records.
failure_points: No first-aid/CPR certification for each employee
Chain-saw chaps/PPE not provided
Untrained employees felling timber

title: Grain Handling Facilities
applicability: Grain elevators, feed mills, flour mills, grain processing, and other facilities handling bulk raw agricultural commodities (dust-explosion and engulfment hazards).
required_elements: Written housekeeping program addressing fugitive grain dust accumulations on floors and surfaces
Hot work permit system in grain handling areas
Preventive maintenance program for mechanical and safety-control equipment
Bin/tank/silo entry permit program (engulfment): testing, lockout of loading, body harness/lifeline, and observer
Contractor notification of known hazards (dust, engulfment, hot work)
Emergency action plan and employee alarm system
training: Training on grain-handling hazards, entry procedures, and emergency response before assignment and annually.
recordkeeping: Retain entry permits, hot work permits, housekeeping schedules, and training records.
failure_points: No written housekeeping program for dust
Bin entry without engulfment controls (harness/observer/loading lockout)
No contractor hazard notification

title: Hazardous Drugs — Safe Handling Program (USP <800> / NIOSH)
applicability: Healthcare and pharmacy settings where employees receive, prepare, administer, or dispose of hazardous drugs (antineoplastics and other NIOSH-listed drugs).
required_elements: Written Hazardous Drug safe-handling plan naming a responsible person and covering the NIOSH hazardous-drug list
Engineering controls: containment primary engineering controls (BSC/CACI) and containment segregated compounding area
PPE: chemo-rated gloves, gowns, eye/face and respiratory protection per activity
Safe receipt, storage, compounding, transport, administration, spill, and waste-disposal procedures
Medical surveillance and exposure-response procedures for potentially exposed staff
Environmental wipe sampling / deactivation-decontamination-cleaning procedures
training: Initial and ongoing competency training for all staff who handle hazardous drugs; documented before independent work.
recordkeeping: Retain the written plan, training/competency records, medical surveillance, and spill/exposure reports.
failure_points: No assessment of containment for the facility's hazardous-drug list
Chemo PPE not specified per activity
No spill kit or exposure-response procedure
notes: USP <800> is enforceable via state boards of pharmacy and OSHA General Duty Clause / HazCom.

title: Tuberculosis (TB) Exposure Control Plan — Healthcare
citation: CDC MMWR 2005 TB Guidelines (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.134 / GDC)
applicability: Healthcare settings and other facilities with reasonably anticipated occupational exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (hospitals, clinics, corrections, long-term care, labs).
required_elements: Written TB infection-control plan with a facility risk assessment and assigned responsibility
Administrative controls: early identification, isolation, and management of persons with suspected/confirmed TB
Environmental controls: airborne infection isolation rooms (negative pressure), ventilation, HEPA/UVGI where used
Respiratory protection program per 1910.134 with fit-tested N95 or higher for exposed staff
TB screening/testing and medical follow-up for employees per facility risk level
training: Initial and periodic TB training for staff with potential exposure; documented.
recordkeeping: Retain the plan, risk assessment, TB screening/medical records (per 1910.1020), and fit-test records.
failure_points: No facility TB risk assessment
No fit-tested respirators for staff entering isolation
No airborne isolation controls

title: Safe Patient Handling and Mobility (SPHM) Program
citation: OSHA General Duty Clause 29 USC 654 / NIOSH; state SPHM statutes
applicability: Healthcare facilities where staff manually lift, transfer, or reposition patients/residents (hospitals, nursing homes, home health, rehab).
required_elements: Written SPHM policy with management commitment and a designated coordinator/committee
Patient handling hazard assessment and mobility/lift assessment per patient
Provision and maintenance of mechanical lift and transfer equipment matched to needs
Minimal manual-lift / no-lift procedures and algorithms
Incident reporting and post-incident review for musculoskeletal injuries
training: Initial and annual training on SPHM equipment and techniques; competency documented.
recordkeeping: Retain assessments, equipment maintenance, training, and injury records.
failure_points: No lift equipment available or maintained
Manual lifting still the default with no assessment
No injury tracking to target high-risk units

title: EPCRA / SARA Title III — Tier II Reporting & Toxic Release Inventory (Form R)
applicability: Facilities storing hazardous chemicals above thresholds (Tier II) and manufacturers/processors/users of listed toxic chemicals above thresholds (TRI/Form R). Also EPCRA release notification.
required_elements: Inventory of hazardous chemicals on site with SDS availability to LEPC/SERC and fire department
Annual Tier II inventory report (by March 1) to SERC, LEPC, and local fire department where thresholds are met
Toxic Release Inventory (Form R / Form A) reporting (by July 1) for listed chemicals above thresholds
Emergency Planning notification and facility coordinator designation where Extremely Hazardous Substances are present
Release notification procedures for reportable quantities
training: Staff assigned to environmental reporting trained on thresholds and deadlines.
recordkeeping: Retain Tier II and Form R submissions and supporting calculations (typically 3 years for TRI).
failure_points: Missed March 1 Tier II or July 1 Form R deadline
Thresholds not evaluated for all listed chemicals
No LEPC/fire department coordination

title: EPA NPDES Industrial Stormwater (MSGP) — Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan
applicability: Industrial facilities in regulated sectors with stormwater discharges associated with industrial activity (distinct from construction CGP). Covered under the EPA MSGP or an equivalent state permit.
required_elements: Written Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) with a pollution prevention team and site description
Identification of potential pollutant sources and industrial materials exposed to stormwater
Control measures / BMPs: good housekeeping, spill prevention, erosion controls, and structural controls
Routine facility inspections and quarterly visual assessments of stormwater discharges
Benchmark and effluent monitoring per applicable sector; corrective action procedures
Employee training and annual comprehensive site compliance evaluation
training: Annual training for staff implementing BMPs and conducting inspections/monitoring.
recordkeeping: Retain the SWPPP, inspection/monitoring records, and corrective actions per permit (typically retain and keep current).
failure_points: SWPPP not site-specific or not kept current
Missed quarterly visual/benchmark monitoring
No corrective action after benchmark exceedance

title: Underground Storage Tanks (UST) Program
applicability: Owners/operators of underground storage tank systems storing petroleum or hazardous substances above regulatory thresholds.
required_elements: Release detection/leak monitoring methods for tanks and piping
Spill and overfill prevention equipment and operation
Corrosion protection and its testing/monitoring
Operator training (Class A/B/C operators) and designation
Release reporting, investigation, and corrective-action procedures
Recordkeeping of testing, monitoring, and walkthrough inspections
training: Class A/B/C UST operator training as required by the implementing agency.
recordkeeping: Retain release-detection, corrosion-protection, and inspection records per 40 CFR 280 (varies 1-3 years by record).
failure_points: No/late release detection records
Untrained UST operators
Failed corrosion protection not corrected

title: Lead Renovation, Repair and Painting (RRP) Rule
applicability: Firms performing renovation, repair, or painting that disturbs lead-based paint in pre-1978 housing and child-occupied facilities (distinct from OSHA lead-in-construction exposure rules).
required_elements: EPA (or authorized state) firm certification
Certified Renovator assigned to each job with training of non-certified workers
Lead-safe work practices: containment, dust minimization, and prohibited practices
Post-renovation cleaning and cleaning verification
Distribution of the EPA lead pamphlet and pre-renovation notification
Recordkeeping of certifications, notifications, and job documentation
training: Certified Renovator initial and refresher training from an EPA-accredited provider.
recordkeeping: Retain renovation records and certifications for at least 3 years.
failure_points: Firm or renovator not certified
No cleaning verification performed
Lead pamphlet/notification not documented

title: Universal Waste Management
applicability: Handlers of universal wastes — batteries, certain pesticides, mercury-containing equipment, lamps, and (in some states) aerosol cans.
required_elements: Identification and proper container management/labeling of universal wastes
Accumulation time limits (generally 1 year) and demonstration of accumulation start date
Employee information/training appropriate to handler status
Response procedures for releases
Off-site shipment to a destination facility with tracking as required
training: Employees informed of proper handling and emergency procedures for the universal wastes on site.
recordkeeping: Retain records demonstrating accumulation dates and shipments.
failure_points: Universal waste over the 1-year accumulation limit
Containers not labeled/closed
No release-response procedure

title: Used Oil Management Standards
applicability: Generators, collection centers, transporters, and processors/re-refiners of used oil (auto/fleet maintenance, industrial equipment, marine).
required_elements: Used oil storage in tanks/containers in good condition, labeled 'Used Oil'
Secondary containment or spill controls for storage areas
Spill/leak response and cleanup procedures
Off-site transport by permitted transporters with EPA ID where required
No mixing of used oil with hazardous waste (rebuttable presumption)
training: Staff trained on used-oil labeling, storage, and spill response.
recordkeeping: Retain shipment and management records as applicable.
failure_points: Containers not labeled 'Used Oil'
No spill controls/secondary containment
Used oil mixed with hazardous waste

title: Risk Management Program (RMP) — Clean Air Act 112(r)
applicability: Facilities with more than a threshold quantity of a listed regulated (flammable or toxic) substance in a process. Complements OSHA PSM (1910.119).
required_elements: Hazard assessment with offsite consequence analysis (worst-case and alternative scenarios) and 5-year accident history
Prevention program (aligned with PSM for Program 3): process safety information, PHA, operating procedures, training, mechanical integrity, MOC, incident investigation
Emergency response program coordinated with local responders
RMP submission to EPA and updates at least every 5 years
Management system with a qualified person accountable for implementation
training: Process operator and emergency-response training consistent with the program level.
recordkeeping: Retain the RMP, PHA, compliance audits, and incident investigation records (generally 5 years).
failure_points: RMP not resubmitted within 5 years
Offsite consequence analysis missing/outdated
Prevention program not coordinated with PSM

title: Medical Services and First Aid — Shipyard
applicability: Shipyard employment — ensures prompt medical attention and first-aid capability at ship repair, shipbuilding, and shipbreaking worksites.
required_elements: Ready availability of medical personnel for advice/consultation
First-aid trained persons when no infirmary/clinic/hospital is in near proximity
First-aid supplies readily available and maintained
Eye-wash/quick-drench facilities where corrosive materials are present
Procedures for prompt transport of injured employees
training: First-aid/CPR training for designated employees, kept current.
recordkeeping: Retain first-aid training certifications and injury records.
failure_points: No first-aid trained person on remote sites
Eyewash absent where corrosives are used
First-aid supplies not maintained

title: Electrical Safety Program (ESP) — Overarching Requirement (NFPA 70E 110)
applicability: Any employer whose employees are exposed to electrical hazards must have a documented electrical safety program that directs activity appropriate to the risk. This is the umbrella the shock, arc-flash, EEWP, and training procedures live under.
required_elements: A documented program that assigns responsibility and directs activity appropriate to the electrical hazard and its associated risk
A risk-assessment procedure that identifies hazards, estimates likelihood and severity, and applies the hierarchy of risk control (elimination first, PPE last)
A job-safety-planning / job-briefing step performed before work with an electrical hazard
Incident-energy / equipment condition information and controls kept current
Auditing: the program is audited at least every 3 years and field work practices are observed at least annually (70E 110.5(M))
training: Employees and their supervisors are trained on the program content relevant to their exposure.
recordkeeping: Keep the written program, the risk-assessment procedure, audit records (program audit every 3 years; field audit annually), and corrective actions.
failure_points: No written electrical safety program at all
Program exists but is never audited / no field observation of work practices
Hierarchy of risk control not applied (jumps straight to PPE)
source: https://www.osha.gov/electrical  (NFPA 70E is the consensus arc-flash method OSHA references; buy the standard at nfpa.org/70E)
notes: NFPA 70E is copyrighted; requirements are stated in Origin's own words with section citations. Point the user to the actual 70E text for exact wording.

title: Establishing an Electrically Safe Work Condition (ESWC / LOTO)
applicability: De-energizing is the default. An ESWC is the verified state that must be created before any work is treated as de-energized. Applies to all conductors and circuit parts to which employees may be exposed.
required_elements: Determine all possible sources of supply to the equipment (use up-to-date drawings/labels)
Open the disconnecting device(s) for each source and, where possible, visually verify the blades/contacts are open
Release stored electrical (capacitors) and mechanical (springs) energy
Apply lockout/tagout in accordance with a documented procedure (ties to 1910.147)
Test-before-touch: use an adequately rated, properly functioning test instrument to verify absence of voltage on all phases; prove the tester on a known live source before and after
Ground where induced voltage or stored energy is a hazard
training: Only qualified persons establish an ESWC; they must be trained on the verification steps and on proving the test instrument.
recordkeeping: LOTO procedure and periodic inspection records; equipment/drawing updates.
failure_points: Treating equipment as dead without a test-before-touch
Not proving the meter on a known source (dead meter reads 'safe' on a live bus)
Missing a second/back-fed source of supply
source: https://www.osha.gov/electrical  (NFPA 70E is the consensus arc-flash method OSHA references; buy the standard at nfpa.org/70E)
notes: Once a verified ESWC exists, the work is no longer 'energized' and the EEWP/boundary/AR-PPE machinery does not apply. Getting to the ESWC is where the shock hazard actually lives.

title: Shock Risk Assessment and Approach Boundaries
applicability: Performed whenever an employee may be exposed to an energized part at 50 V or more. Determines how close a person may approach and what shock PPE is required.
required_elements: Identify the nominal system voltage of the exposed part
Determine the limited approach boundary (the distance beyond which an unqualified person must not cross without a qualified escort and PPE)
Determine the restricted approach boundary (only a qualified person, with a documented plan and shock PPE, may cross)
Select shock PPE: rubber insulating gloves (with leather protectors) and insulated/insulating tools rated for the voltage
Estimate the likelihood and severity of a shock and apply controls
training: Qualified persons trained to look up the correct boundaries for the voltage and to don voltage-rated gloves and use insulated tools.
recordkeeping: Glove test records (retest cycle typically 6 months); tool inspection records.
failure_points: Using the wrong voltage class of gloves
No restricted approach boundary observed while reaching into a live panel
Untested / expired rubber insulating gloves
source: https://www.osha.gov/electrical  (NFPA 70E is the consensus arc-flash method OSHA references; buy the standard at nfpa.org/70E)
notes: Exact boundary distances live in NFPA 70E Table 130.4(E)(a)/(b) by voltage — Origin cites the table and voltage but does not reproduce the copyrighted distance values. Look them up in the current 70E.

title: Arc-Flash Risk Assessment and Incident-Energy Analysis
applicability: Required before working within the arc-flash boundary on energized equipment, or when the equipment condition (doors open, covers off) exposes an arc-flash hazard.
required_elements: Determine the arc-flash boundary — the distance at which incident energy equals 1.2 cal/cm2 (the onset of a second-degree burn)

Choose ONE method and do not mix them on a task: (a) incident-energy analysis — calculate incident energy in cal/cm2 (commonly via IEEE 1584 / an engineering study) and select AR PPE with an arc rating at or above it; or (b) the PPE-category (table) method in 70E 130.7(C)(15)
Account for equipment condition and maintenance (an un-maintained breaker that fails to clear raises incident energy)
Reflect results on the equipment arc-flash label and keep the study current (re-study when the electrical system changes)
training: Persons performing the analysis are qualified/competent in the method used; field workers are trained to read the label and select PPE accordingly.
recordkeeping: The arc-flash / incident-energy study, the label schedule, and the re-study trigger log.
failure_points: No incident-energy study and no PPE-category basis — boundaries are guessed
Study never updated after transformer/breaker/utility changes
Mixing the two methods on the same task
source: https://www.osha.gov/electrical  (NFPA 70E is the consensus arc-flash method OSHA references; buy the standard at nfpa.org/70E)
notes: 1.2 cal/cm2 (second-degree-burn threshold) is a published scientific value and is stated as such. The PPE-category selection tables (130.7(C)(15)) are copyrighted 70E content — cite them, do not reproduce.

title: Arc-Rated PPE and Insulated Tool Selection
applicability: Applies whenever an employee works inside the arc-flash boundary or where a shock hazard exists.
required_elements: Select arc-rated (AR) clothing and equipment with an arc rating (ATPV or EBT, in cal/cm2) at or above the assessed incident energy — or the PPE ensemble specified by the chosen PPE category

Cover the arc-flash hazard body zones: AR shirt/pants or coverall, AR face shield with balaclava or an arc-flash hood, hard hat, safety glasses, hearing protection, and heavy-duty leather (or AR) gloves
Rubber insulating gloves with leather protectors, rated for the system voltage, for shock protection
No meltable synthetic fabrics (nylon, polyester, acetate) as underlayers next to skin
Inspect PPE before use; keep AR garments clean and un-modified (repairs must preserve arc rating)
training: Workers trained to read the label/PPE category and don the correct ensemble; trained on inspection and care.
recordkeeping: Rubber-goods (glove/sleeve) electrical test records; PPE inspection log.
failure_points: AR clothing rating below the incident energy at the task
Meltable synthetics worn under AR clothing
Voltage-rated gloves used without leather protectors or past test date
source: https://www.osha.gov/electrical  (NFPA 70E is the consensus arc-flash method OSHA references; buy the standard at nfpa.org/70E)
notes: Exact PPE ensembles per category are in NFPA 70E Table 130.7(C)(15) — cite, do not copy.

title: Energized Electrical Work Permit (EEWP)
applicability: Required when work will be performed on or near exposed energized parts inside the restricted approach boundary or the arc-flash boundary and the equipment is NOT placed in an electrically safe work condition.
required_elements: A written permit that describes the circuit/equipment and the specific work
Justification why de-energizing is infeasible or introduces a greater hazard (energized work is only allowed on these two grounds)
The shock and arc-flash risk assessment results: boundaries and required PPE
Safe work practices, the means to restrict unqualified access, and evidence of a job briefing
Authorized-approval signatures (a level of management above the worker) before work begins
Defined exemptions: testing, troubleshooting, and voltage measurement by a qualified person in appropriate PPE do not require a written EEWP but still require the risk assessment and PPE
training: Qualified persons and the approving manager trained on when a permit is required and how to complete it.
recordkeeping: Retain completed EEWPs (commonly per project or a fixed retention term) as proof energized work was justified and controlled.
failure_points: Energized work performed with no permit and no infeasibility justification
Permit signed by the worker only (no independent management authorization)
Treating routine energized tasks as exempt without doing the risk assessment
source: https://www.osha.gov/electrical  (NFPA 70E is the consensus arc-flash method OSHA references; buy the standard at nfpa.org/70E)
notes: Origin ships a fillable EEWP form template. The 'infeasible or greater hazard' test is the crux reviewers check — production convenience is not a valid justification.

title: Arc-Flash Equipment Labeling
applicability: Applies to switchboards, panelboards, industrial control panels, meter socket enclosures, and motor control centers in other than dwelling units that are likely to require examination, adjustment, servicing, or maintenance while energized.
required_elements: Field-marked label on the equipment showing nominal system voltage
The arc-flash boundary
At least one of: available incident energy and the corresponding working distance, OR the minimum arc rating of clothing, OR the required PPE category (one method, consistent with the study)
Labels legible, durable, and updated when the study changes
training: Field workers trained to read the label and select boundaries/PPE from it.
recordkeeping: Label schedule tied to the arc-flash study; re-label log when the system changes.
failure_points: Unlabeled gear that is serviced energized
Label data inconsistent with the current study
notes: The label duty is OSHA-enforceable via 1910.303 design requirements plus the general duty clause; 70E 130.5(H) specifies the content.

title: Qualified vs. Unqualified Person — Electrical Training
applicability: Defines who may do electrical work and what training each class needs. Prequal reviewers routinely ask for the qualified-person roster and training records.
required_elements: Definition of a qualified person: trained and demonstrably able to identify and avoid the electrical hazards, determine nominal voltage, use PPE and insulated tools, and apply approach boundaries — qualification is task- and equipment-specific
Definition of an unqualified person and the limits on their exposure (must stay outside the limited approach boundary unless escorted and protected)
Training content: safety-related work practices, ESWC/LOTO, boundaries, arc-flash, PPE, and emergency response including release/resuscitation
Retraining at least every 3 years, and when new equipment/procedures are introduced, when practices are not followed, or when an audit finds a deficiency
Documentation of each employee, the training content, the date, and demonstrated proficiency
training: Delivered by a competent instructor; proficiency demonstrated, not just attended.
recordkeeping: Qualified-person roster; training records with content, date, trainer, and retrain-due dates.
failure_points: Calling someone 'qualified' with no documented training or demonstrated skill
Training older than the 3-year retrain cycle
No emergency-response / CPR component for those exposed to shock hazards
notes: Qualification is not a blanket title — a person can be qualified on one system/task and unqualified on another.

title: Determining Work-Relatedness (and the Exceptions)
applicability: The first gate before any case is recorded. A case is work-related if an event or exposure in the work environment caused or contributed to the condition, or significantly aggravated a pre-existing condition.
required_elements: Apply the presumption: injuries/illnesses arising from the work environment are presumed work-related unless a listed exception applies

Know the exceptions (1904.5(b)(2)): e.g., present as a member of the public; symptoms surface at work but result solely from a non-work event; voluntary wellness/health-club activity; eating/drinking own food; personal grooming/self-medication for a non-work condition; common cold or flu; certain mental illness cases without a professional opinion linking to work
Handle travel-status and work-at-home cases per the special rules in 1904.5(b)(6)-(7)
Decide 'new case' vs. continuation of an old case under 1904.6
recordkeeping: Document the basis for any not-work-related determination in case of an audit.
failure_points: Recording (or not recording) without applying the 1904.5(b)(2) exceptions
Treating a recurrence of an old injury as a new case
notes: Work-relatedness errors are a top driver of a wrong TRIR — both over- and under-recording distort a prequal score.

title: General Recording Criteria — Is the Case Recordable?
applicability: Once a case is work-related and a new case, 1904.7 decides recordability. This is the decision the entire TRIR/DART calculation rests on.
required_elements: Record if the case results in ANY of: death; days away from work; restricted work or transfer to another job; medical treatment beyond first aid; loss of consciousness; or a significant injury/illness diagnosed by a physician or other licensed health care professional
Use the closed 'first aid' list in 1904.7(b)(5)(ii) — anything NOT on that list is 'medical treatment beyond first aid' and is recordable (e.g., prescription meds, sutures, rigid splints)
Count calendar days (not workdays) for days-away and restricted/transfer; begin counting the day AFTER the injury; cap the total at 180 days
If a case moves from restricted to days-away, update the classification to the more serious outcome
Special recording criteria (1904.8-.12): needlesticks/sharps, medical removal, hearing loss (STS + 25 dB), TB, and (where in effect) MSDs
recordkeeping: Record within 7 calendar days of learning of the case; keep the 300 Log current.
failure_points: Misclassifying prescription medication or sutures as 'first aid' (they are recordable)
Counting workdays instead of calendar days
Not capping days at 180
notes: The single most important record in the KB for TRIR accuracy. When in doubt, the first-aid list is exhaustive — if a treatment is not on it, it is recordable.

title: OSHA 300 Log, 301 Report, and Privacy Concern Cases
applicability: Governs the forms themselves: what goes on the 300 Log, the 301 Incident Report, and how to protect employee privacy for sensitive cases.
required_elements: Maintain an OSHA 300 Log (or equivalent) for each establishment expected to be in operation for a year or more; enter each recordable case within 7 days
Complete an OSHA 301 Incident Report (or equivalent such as a workers' comp first report) for each recordable case within 7 days

Privacy concern cases — do NOT enter the employee's name on the 300 Log; write 'privacy case' and keep a separate confidential list: injuries to intimate body parts/reproductive system, sexual assaults, mental illnesses, HIV/hepatitis/TB, needlesticks/sharps involving contamination, and any case where the employee voluntarily requests name omission
Give employees and former employees access to their own records on request (1904.35)
recordkeeping: Keep the separate privacy-case list secure; provide records to employees/reps per 1904.35 and to government per 1904.40.
failure_points: Employee name shown on a privacy-concern case
301 (or equivalent) not completed within 7 days
notes: A separate confidential list is mandatory for privacy cases — a 300 Log that names them is a recordkeeping violation.

title: OSHA 300A Annual Summary — Certification and Posting
applicability: The year-end obligation. Required even for an establishment with zero recordable cases (post the form showing zeros).
required_elements: At year end, review the 300 Log for completeness and accuracy and correct any deficiencies
Total the columns and enter them on the OSHA 300A Annual Summary, including average employees and total hours worked

Certify the summary: a company executive (owner/officer, highest-ranking company official at the site, or that person's immediate supervisor) signs certifying the log was examined and the summary is correct
Post the certified 300A in a conspicuous place from February 1 through April 30 of the year following the year covered
Post even if there were zero recordable cases
recordkeeping: Retain the certified 300A for 5 years; keep the certifier's signature.
failure_points: 300A certified by a safety manager/HR clerk instead of a company executive
Posted late, removed early, or not posted because there were zero cases
Hours worked or average employees left blank (breaks TRIR calculation)
notes: 'Company executive' is defined narrowly in 1904.32(b)(4) — the most common recordkeeping citation and a frequent prequal rejection.

title: Reporting Fatalities and Severe Injuries to OSHA
applicability: Applies to ALL employers — including those otherwise partially exempt from recordkeeping. Separate from the 300 Log.
required_elements: Report a work-related fatality within 8 hours of learning of it
Report a work-related in-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye within 24 hours of learning of it
Report via the OSHA 800-number, the online reporting form, or the nearest area office
Fatality reportable if it occurs within 30 days of the incident; in-patient hospitalization/amputation/eye loss reportable if it occurs within 24 hours of the incident
Provide: establishment name, location/time of incident, type of event, number affected, names, and a contact
recordkeeping: Keep a record of the report made (date, time, who reported, confirmation).
failure_points: Missing the 8-hour (fatality) / 24-hour (hospitalization, amputation, eye) window
Assuming a partially exempt employer need not report (they must)
notes: An amputation includes fingertip amputations with bone loss. Late reporting is a distinct, separately citable violation.

title: Electronic Submission of Injury Data (ITA)
applicability: Determines which establishments must upload their injury data to OSHA's Injury Tracking Application (ITA) each year, and what they upload.
required_elements: Establishments with 250+ employees (in industries required to keep records) submit the 300A electronically
Establishments with 20-249 employees in designated higher-hazard industries (Appendix A to Subpart E) submit the 300A

Since the 2024 rule: establishments with 100+ employees in the highest-hazard industries (Appendix B) submit the 300 Log and 301 Incident Report data in addition to the 300A, including the establishment's legal company name
Annual deadline: March 2 for the prior calendar year
Submit through the ITA web portal (manual entry, CSV upload, or API)
recordkeeping: Retain the ITA submission confirmation; reconcile submitted totals to the posted 300A.
failure_points: Not knowing the establishment's industry falls in Appendix A/B
Missing the March 2 deadline
Counts submitted don't match the posted 300A
notes: Coverage is by establishment size and industry, not just company size. The 2024 rule expanded case-detail (300/301) submission for large high-hazard establishments.

title: Retention and Updating of Records
applicability: How long the forms are kept and the duty to keep them accurate during that window.
required_elements: Retain the OSHA 300 Log, the privacy-case list, the 300A Annual Summary, and the 301 Incident Reports for 5 years following the end of the calendar year those records cover
During the 5-year retention period, update the stored 300 Log to include newly discovered recordable cases and to reflect changes to recorded cases (the 300A does not have to be updated)
On business transfer, the receiving employer must retain the prior records for the remainder of the period
recordkeeping: Store all 5 years accessibly for employee access (1904.35) and government requests (1904.40, within 4 business hours).
failure_points: Discarding logs before the 5-year window
Not updating a prior-year 300 Log when a case later becomes recordable
notes: Government access requests under 1904.40 must be met within 4 business hours — retention alone is not enough; the records must be retrievable.

title: OSHA Injury & Illness Recordkeeping Program
applicability: A written program that documents HOW the company keeps its OSHA injury/illness records accurately and on time. Prequal platforms (ISN RAVS, Avetta, Veriforce, PEC) accept a recordkeeping procedure as evidence the TRIR/DART they grade is reliable.
required_elements: Assigned recordkeeper and backup, with authority and training
Work-relatedness and recordability decision procedure (1904.5 / 1904.7), including use of the first-aid list and day-counting rules
OSHA 300 Log and 301 Incident Report procedure — entered within 7 calendar days
Privacy-concern-case handling (separate confidential list; no name on the 300 Log)
OSHA 300A annual review, executive certification, and Feb 1-Apr 30 posting
Severe-injury reporting procedure (fatality 8 hr; hospitalization/amputation/eye 24 hr) with the reporting method and contacts
ITA electronic submission procedure and the March 2 deadline (if the establishment is covered)
5-year retention, updating during retention, and employee/government access
training: The recordkeeper (and backup) is trained on the 1904.5/.7 decision tree, the first-aid list, day counting, privacy cases, posting, reporting windows, and ITA submission.
recordkeeping: Retain 300, 300A, 301, and the privacy-case list for 5 years following the year covered; keep ITA confirmations and the reporting log.
failure_points: 300A not certified by a company executive
Recordability decisions inconsistent (drives a wrong TRIR)
Late severe-injury reporting
No named, trained recordkeeper
notes: This is the written-program companion to the 1904 reference records. Naming its template program-osha-recordkeeping-program.md auto-wires it to the gap-draft engine.
